title: NHS-R/NHS.pycom Conference Workshop 2023: Level Up Your Plots!
details: Level up your plots: Using colour, annotations, text hierarchy and other tricks to make your data story stand out with Cara Thompson Wednesday 04th October 2023 Workshop Content: You are encouraged to bring a ggplot of your own making to the workshop – we will code our way towards a better version of it together. Copy the code from the Quarto slides and reuse at will! Here’s a list of the packages I’ll be using: Available on CRAN: - Tidyverse - Palmerpenguins - Systemfonts - monochromeR - ggtext - geomtextpath. Available from GitHub: - colorblindr - See instructions at: github.com/clauswilke/colorblindr And here’s what we’ll cover: - Picking intuitive colours to make our graphs more memorable - Making our colour choices (and text) as accessible as we can - With a review of the latest Nightingale In Print Accessibility guidelines - Optimising text hierarchy in our plots, and packing our work up as a reusable ggplot theme - Reducing unnecessary eye movement and cognitive load by being careful about what text we include/exclude, and where we put it - Adding in-plot annotations to highlight important patterns. By the end of the session, you’ll have… - A solid set of colours that you’ve tested against accessibility criteria - A reusable ggplot theme with optimised text hierarchy - A decluttered plot that makes the most of the visual space available - Additional tips and tricks for adding in-plot annotations - A set of resources you can return to when working on new graphs!

title: NHS-R/NHS.pycom Conference Workshop 2023: Create your own API with Python and FastAPI
details: Create your own API with Python and FastAPI with YiWen Hon Monday 02nd October 2023 Workshop Content: The objective of this workshop is to introduce Python users to the FastAPI package and show them how to build their own API, using free and open source tools. APIs are a great way of making machine learning models more accessible to a wider audience, reducing the technical barrier to entry. We will begin with an overview of what APIs are and how they can be interrogated, and a revision of basic concepts such as the JSON data format, and how it is comprised of the lists and dict types. We will practice using the requests library to query a simple API endpoint. We will then move on to using FastAPI to build a very basic endpoint, using the Uvicorn package to test if it works on the local machine. After that, we will build a more complex API endpoint that accepts parameters, again testing if it works on the local machine. Depending on the progress of participants, we can also touch on more complex concepts such as validating parameters, POST requests, and documentation. The workshop will finish with suggestions for how the API can be made publicly available, with an overview of some hosting solutions, and common considerations such as authentication and security. By the end of the workshop, participants should be able to: - Query APIs using the Python requests library - Create a basic RESTful API using FastAPI - Test their API locally using Uvicorn.

title: NHS-R/NHS.pycom Conference Workshop 2023: Modelling non-linear data with Generalized Additive Models
details: Modelling non-linear data with Generalized Additive Models (GAMs), using the mgcv package with Chris Mainey Friday 13th October 2023 Workshop Content: This workshop is a follow-on from my talk at last year’s NHS-R conference on modelling ‘wiggly’ data using Generalized Additive Models. Regression models are a great approach for modelling relationships, but they make certain assumptions about linear relationships that don’t always hold true in real-world datasets. The workshop is aimed at people who have some experience of regression modelling and want to take it further, learning a more advanced and flexible class of modelling that also applies to non-linear data. This workshop will introduce the class of models (explaining a GAM as a GLM with smooth functions of predictors). We will then walk through a simple healthcare based example of a GAM. We will discuss how to interpret the GAM, assess whether the fit is good, and look at ways to visualise the smooth functions. We will then take a detour through what the smoothers actually do, using piece-wise cubic splines, as our example. We will finish the workshop with a more complicated example, asking attendees to fit the model, examine the smoothers and answer a couple of questions about them. Please be advised that this course is an advanced regression modelling course, and it is essential that attendees have some experience of fitting regression models in R to understand the application of GAMs. Slides

title: NHS-R/NHS.pycom Conference Workshop 2023: Introduction to Version Control (Git/GitHub)
details: Introduction to Version Control (Git/GitHub) with Joseph Wilson and Helen Richardson Thursday 12th October 2023 GitHub repository: Workshop Content: Building upon the success of the 2022 Introduction to Version Control (Git/GitHub) workshop, this day-long course returns to equip participants with essential skills in version control using Git and GitHub. This workshop emphasizes a more agnostic approach, accommodating both R and Python users, with the course curriculum focusing on interacting with Git through the command line. However, some supplementary materials and support will be available for those interacting with Git through RStudio and VSCode. Key topics covered in this workshop include: - Git Basics: Participants will grasp the fundamental concepts of repositories, branches (alternate versions of the repository), and the process of accessing/cloning repositories. They will gain practice in creating branches, making changes, and pushing changes to GitHub. - Git Collaboration: Collaboration is crucial in version control, and participants will learn how to submit Pull Requests (PRs), assign reviewers, and explore PR options, ensuring efficient and seamless collaboration among team members. In addition, participants will be shown how to resolve conflicting changes together. - Extra: Creating a Repository on GitHub: Attendees will also gain practical insights into creating repositories directly on GitHub, enabling them to establish a strong foundation for their version control projects. The primary learning objectives of this workshop are for participants to learn all the basics to start utilizing version control in their projects. Participants will be able to complete practical exercises to practice merging changes from branches together and managing cases when conflicting changes arise.

title: NHS-R/NHS.pycom Conference Workshop 2023: Data Visualisation with Seaborn
details: Data Visualisation with Seaborn with Parisa Gregg Thursday 05th October 2023 Workshop Content: Over the last few decades, a plethora of Python packages have been developed to tackle a range of data visualisation problems. This tutorial will provide a hands-on introduction to Seaborn, a fantastic open-source plotting library that builds on the Matplotlib package. Seaborn allows complex data visualisations to be created simply and easily, whilst also improving on the default look and feel of Matplotlib figures. This hands-on workshop will cover: - Seaborn’s statistical functions (kernel density estimation, regression models, etc) - creating multi-plot grids with Seaborn - customisation of Seaborn figures with Matplotlib. By the end, you will be able to: - use a range of techniques for communicating your data insights - leverage the best aspects of Seaborn and Matplotlib to create beautiful graphics with concise code. No previous experience in Seaborn is necessary for this tutorial. However, basic familiarity with Pandas DataFrames and plotting with Matplotlib would be useful. This workshop will be run using an online environment with all the dependencies and libraries pre-installed.

title: NHS-R/NHS.pycom Conference Workshop 2023: Introduction to R and R Studio (Part 2)
details: Introduction to R and R Studio (Part 2) with Zoë Turner Tuesday 03rd October 2023 Workshop Content: This is a great opportunity for anyone who is interested in data analysis using Excel, SQL, Access or uses statistical programmes like SPSS to get started with R and R Studio. After this course, you will: - See examples of R in producing healthcare related visualisations and use publicly available healthcare data to answer questions. - Recognise and understand key terms often used by users of R. - Interact with R using the RStudio environment. - Learn how to set up some of the accessibility features of RStudio. - Take charge of their workflow using RStudio projects. - Import data into R using csv files (other data sources will be discussed). - Carry out data manipulation using simple steps to solve complex problems. - Join multiple tables together. - Produce and save plots using ggplot2. - Learn how to find more information on functions within R packages. - Open an RMarkdown template and learn how to get started in producing an integrated text and code report. - Take away ideas for continuing learning after the course. Pre-requisites: No prior knowledge of R is required; however, it is assumed that you will have a moderate level of computer literacy. For example, you will be able to navigate to drives and files and be confident in searching for solutions to technical problems on the internet. You will work with, or have an interest in, data.

title: NHS-R/NHS.pycom Conference Workshop 2023: Intermediate R follow on from "Intro to R and RStudio"
details: Intermediate R – follow on from ‘Introduction to R and R Studio’ with Simon Wellesley-Miller Friday 06th October 2023 Workshop Content: In this workshop we will be looking at applying some of the knowledge learned in the ‘Introduction to R and R Studio’ workshop and applying the methods learned to practical questions. Key topics: - Further uses of dplyr with conditional statements - Use of group_by and mutate to create sub totals and percentages across groups - Date manipulation - Use of stringr to clean up messy strings - Practice with charting in GGplot and simple conversion to Plotly - How to create pretty tables. Edited with Clipchamp

title: NHS-R Conference Workshop: Building a TidyModels model from scratch – 01/11/22
details: Led by Gary Hutson, Head of Machine Learning, Crisp 1st November 2022 Here we will learn how to build a TidyModels classification model from scratch RPubs document: About the course: The art and science of building a machine model from scratch and then pushing this into production as a consumable endpoint with Plumber R package. title: NHS-R Conference Workshop: Introduction to Interactive plotting with R – 03/11/22
details: Introduction to Interactive plotting with R Thursday 3rd November 2022, Led by Annie Yu, Epidemiological Programmer, Hertfordshire County Council Pre-requisites: Some introductory experience with R About the course: The workshop will cover creating interactive graphs using plotly and echarts4r packages as well as the motivations behind using interactive graphs in reports and apps. It will go through the basic syntax of each package and how to create basic bar, scatter, and line graphs while customising the hover labels, legends, and themes. I will go through additional functionalities of each package, such as adding buttons, additional layers, and grouping/linkage between graphs. The session will have some basic exercises with optional additional challenges to create complex plots and render it using Rmarkdown.

title: NHS-R Workshop: Level up your plots! - 04/11/22
details: Level up your plots: tips and tricks for creating compelling data visualisations in R Friday 4th November 202 Led by Cara Thompson, Freelance Data Consultant - Building Stories with Data Pre-requisites: It would be helpful for participants to have a basic grasp of: - creating a plot with ggplot2 - data wrangling within the tidyverse About the course: “Ooh, nice ggplot!” is never the reaction we’re after when we’ve spent time putting together a plot in R. Instead, we want the plot to help readers engage well with the key patterns in the data. This workshop will give delegates a tour of the ways we can use ggplot to create compelling publication-ready data visualisations. We will code our way from a basic plot to a plot which presents a clear story in an aesthetically pleasing way, and delegates will be encouraged to apply the tips and tricks we explore together to their own plots. During the workshop, we will cover: - a quick overview of foundational ggplot concepts - design principles we can apply to our datavisualisations - how to choose and apply a bespoke colour scheme, both to the text and to the data in the plot - how to change the fonts and colours of text - how to create polished annotations to support the main story of the plot -how to export high quality plots for publication - sources of dataviz inspiration for future projects These tips will be applicable to a wide range of plot types, to maximise relevance to delegates working with different types of data. They will be encouraged to ask questions and apply these tips to their own plots during the workshop, with the aim of equipping them with the design and coding know-how to create compelling datavisualisations with their own data. Learning objectives By the end of the workshop, delegates will be able to: - describe basic design principles that they can apply to datavisualisations - describe the basic components of a ggplot plot - apply a colour scheme they crafted themselves to their own plots - write code which modifies the different default ggplot elements - work with fonts, colours and alignments to make the text of their plot an integral part of the visualisation - export publication-ready plots

title: NHS-R Webinar: Tips and tricks learnt from building production {shiny} apps  - 07/11/22
details: Tips and tricks learnt from building production {shiny} apps Monday 7th November Delivered by Colin Fay, Data Scientist & R Hacker at ThinkR About the webinar: The road to a production-ready software is always a bumpy road. Whatever you do, you can always expect the unexpected. But the good news is that at the end of the day, many of the issues faced along the road from project init to deployment can be avoided, provided you follow a set of good practices. In this talk, Colin will cover some of the tips and tricks he has learnt from years of building {shiny} applications for production, and some of the patterns he now follows that helps him manage a {shiny} application project from start to finish.

title: NHS-R Workshop: Working with databases in R - 23//11/22
details: Working with databases in R Wednesday 23rd November 2022 Led by Christopher Maronga,m R Programmer, University of Oxford About the course: The first step in any data handling process is loading data into your working tool regardless of the form and media of storage. Relational databases such as RMySQL and web-based databases such as REDCap have gained popularity as efficient and cost-effective storage of small – medium data. In this workshop, I am going to walk you through key steps in extracting and using data store in these platforms using R statistical software with the aid of user-developed Application Programming Interfaces (API’s). Learning objectives: Efficiently connect R to Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS) Query data stored in any RDBMS from within R/Rstudio using dplyr and SQL syntax Connect and querying data from Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) database How to secure your API while working on collaborative projects.

title: NHS-R Workshop: PHM ExploreR An open source tool for Population Health Management  - 24/11/22
details: PHM ExploreR: An open source tool for Population Health Management Thursday 24th November 2022 Led by Andras Varady, Forensic Cancer Pathway Data Scientist, NHS Bristol, North Somerset and South Gloucestershire CCG About the course: The workshop will introduce delegates to the PHM ExploreR: a versatile R Shiny tool created for exploring Population Health and facilitating Population Health Management (PHM) in healthcare systems. PHM is of increasingly high interest within the NHS, but many Business Intelligence departments lack the appropriate tools to keep pace with this rapidly growing field. For NHS analysts, the PHM ExploreR aims to reduce reliance on Excel solutions and management consultancies offering bespoke pieces of work, and enable users to independently and interactively explore the key areas of PHM, such as Population Segmentation and Risk Stratification. The workshop will start by describing the data requirements of the tool, and introduce the synthetic linked dataset used for demonstration. This will also cover the data required for maximum effectiveness of the tool. The workshop will then move on to cover the full functionality of the suite, including: A number of summary graphs and statistics to provide a high level overview of the population. A series of segmentation methods, including Bridges to Health and data-driven methods such as decision trees and clustering methods. Patient-level ‘theoplots’, charting activity utilisation for individuals across multiple healthcare settings. Regression-based risk stratification for analysing and predicting differences in patient activity utilisation and spend.

title: NHS-R Workshop - Regression Modelling in R - 24/11/22
details: Introduction to Regression Modelling Thursday 24th November 2022 Led by Chris Mainey, Deputy Director of Specialist Analytics at North Central London Integrated Care Board Pre-requisites: Some introductory experience with R About the course: This session will focus on how to fit regression models in R, the most common form of statistical modelling. We will examine the essential theory underpinning these models, then fit linear models with a single predictor, then multiple predictors and look at how to interpret them Resources GitHub:

title: NHS-R Workshop: Fitting Distributions in R - 25/11/22
details: Fitting distributions in R Friday 25th November 2022 Led by Dr Sean Manzi, Research Fellow in Applied Healthcare Modelling and Analysis, University of Exeter College of Medicine and Health Pre-requisites: A basic understanding of how to use R About the course: This session will begin by introducing probability distributions, the different types of distribution and why we use them in data science. We will then move on to an overview of the distribution fitting process and how to implement this in R using the ‘fitdistrplus’ and ‘actuar’ packages. As we proceed through the distribution fitting process, we will discuss some of the theory around the techniques used to fit a distribution to a data set. There will be the opportunity to practice generating data from and fitting data to different distributions. Finally, we will explore the use of a shiny based app to help streamline your day-to-day distribution fitting activities.

title: NHS-R Workshop: Shiny (Part 1 of 2) November 2021
details: Facilitator: Chris Beeley, Senior Data Scientist, Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust Summary: Shiny is an programming framework for R that allows you to build dynamic and interactive dashboards for the web with no knowledge of HTML, CSS, or JavaScript. It allows R programmers to very easily allow their users to interact with analyses written in R. This course will teach you Shiny all the way from writing your very first application to writing a full fledged dashboard with real NHS data in, and cover good practice in Shiny development. The course finishes with a preview of advanced methods for those curious to learn more. Pre-requisites: Intermediate knowledge of R and RMarkdown is essential

title: NHS-R Workshop: Introduction to changepoint analysis with R-  November 2021
details: Facilitator: Dr Rebecca Killick Associate Professor in the Mathematics & Statistics department at Lancaster University Summary: This workshop introduces participants to the analysis of changepoint models (also known as time series segmentation or structural changes). The course is aimed at those with an interest in discovering methods for models that include changepoints. It will be interactive and use packages available on CRAN. Following the course participants will be able to: - recognise datasets that potentially contain changepoints - identify appropriate changepoint methods dependent on the type of change suspected - perform changepoint analyses using a variety of techniques in R - summarise and evaluate results of a changepoint analysis Pre-requisites: Basic working knowledge of R and statistical modelling is assumed

title: NHS-R Workshop: Further changepoint analysis techniques –December 2021
details: Facilitator: Dr Rebecca Killick Associate Professor in the Mathematics & Statistics department at Lancaster University Summary: ‘Further changepoint analysis techniques’ workshop builds upon the introduction to changepoint course and that knowledge will be assumed. We will focus on more advanced and recently developed techniques such as how to incorporate: - covariates - seasonality - dependence / autocorrelation - multivariate data Pre-requisites: This workshop builds upon the introduction to changepoint course and that knowledge will be assumed

title: Introduction to Machine Learning and Image Processing with R, December 2021
details: Facilitators: Santosh Kumar and Bruno Petrungaro, The Health Economics Unit Summary: This workshop covers the basics of image processing, classical machine learning with R. Topics in machine learning include an introduction to machine learning, the difference between machine learning and AI, Machine learning models, overfitting in machine learning models, applications of machine learning in the healthcare, and machine learning with R. Topics in image processing include the basics of image processing, including conventions of image representation, visualization, common transformations, and filtering operations, and common methods for image classification. Pre-requisites: Basic mathematics, Beginner R programming, Basic data structure

title: Statistical process control charts with R - Jacob Anhøj, November 2021
details: Date: Thursday 4th November 2021 Statistical process control charts with R One day Workshop: Masterclass for R programmers Facilitators: Jacob Anhøj, Medical Doctor, Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen, Denmark and Zoë Turner, Senior Information Analyst, Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust Summary: This full-day masterclass is for R programmers who want to learn statistical process control (SPC) for continuous quality improvement. In this masterclass you will learn the tools, most notably the process control chart, which is a simple an elegant graph that helps to distinguish between common and special cause variation in processes in time or space. Pre-requisites: are familiar with the basic ideas of SPC, specifically the distinction between common cause and special cause variation; have experience using the R programming language to manipulate, analyse, and plot data; understand basic statistical concepts including probability, population, sample, distribution, and measures of central tendency and dispersion.

title: Reproducible computation at scale in R with targets, Will Landau, November 2021
details: Facilitator: Will Landau, Eli Lilly and Company – USA Data science can be slow. A single round of statistical computation can take several minutes, hours, or even days to complete. The targets R package keeps results up to date and reproducible while minimizing the number of expensive tasks that actually run. targets arranges the steps of your pipeline, skips costly runtime for steps that are already up to date, runs the rest with optional implicit parallel computing, abstracts files as R objects, and shows tangible evidence that the output matches the underlying code and data. In other words, the package saves time while increasing your ability to trust the results. This hands-on workshop teaches targets using a realistic case study Pre-requisites: Some introductory experience with R

title: NHS-R Webinar: Building Multiple Page Shiny Apps with {brochure} - February 2022
details: Join Colin Fay for the NHS-R Webinar - Building Multiple Page Shiny Apps with {brochure} Presenter: Colin Fay, Data Science Engineering at ThinkR Summary: How about we take a step back and think about the way we've been building {shiny} apps so far? What can we learn from the way web apps are built in other languages? What do we actually need when building a web app? And how can we apply the answers to these questions to the way we build our apps with {shiny}? In this talk, Colin will present {brochure}, a package that brings native multi-page support for {shiny}, and demonstrate how you can use it to build an app that will feature all the things you'll traditionally find in a classical web app: multiple endpoint, cookie support, HTTP status codes and methods, and all the cool tools the web developers have been using to build the web.

title: NHS-R Webinar : Strategic Health Asset Planning and Evaluation (SHAPE) - March 2022
details: Join Barbara Coyle for the NHS-R Webinar - Strategic Health Asset Planning and Evaluation (SHAPE) Date: Wednesday 16th March, 1.00 pm – 2.00 pm Presenter: Barbara Coyle, Associate Director at Public Health England Strategic Health Asset Planning and Evaluation (SHAPE) is a web enabled, evidence based application which informs and supports the strategic planning of services and physical assets across a whole health economy. The application contains a number of key indicators covering a range of topics including public health, primary care and demography. Each indicator can be mapped and is linked with information on the location of healthcare assets such as GPs, hospitals, dentists and pharmacies. As well as providing analyses vital for overall strategic planning across whole health economies, SHAPE can be used for numerous more specific planning purposes. These include: Mapping local populations by age, ethnicity, socio-economic status, primary care and public health factors Comparing your local population with other areas Siting new facilities and its impact on populations (with a focus on inequalities) PCN and GP practice primary care data such as QOF, registered populations, prescription activity and workforce Developing a repository of organisation and site estate information Covid vaccination mapping and access analysis Comprehensive travel time analysis for every NHS site Access to SHAPE is free and you can register for access here:

title: NHS-R January 2023 Webinar:  Create reproducible and accessible spreadsheets with {a11ytables}
details: NHS-R Webinar: January 2023 Topic: Create reproducible and accessible spreadsheets with {a11ytables} Delivered by: Matt Dray, Analyst, Analysis & Insight – Cabinet Office Wednesday 18th January 202 About the webinar: The Reproducible Analytical Pipelines (RAP) movement has revolutionised data processing in the UK’s public sector. Civil service analysts are using wholly code-driven approaches to generate official statistics with greater speed, efficiency and reproducibility. But there’s a bottleneck: there’s no unified R solution to autogenerate spreadsheet outputs that meet the Government Statistical Service’s best practice guidelines. This is a problem: creating outputs with time-consuming point-and-click methods defeats the benefits of RAP, while a lack of consistency and accessibility of outputs can drive down trust and usability. To fill this gap I’ve created the {a11ytables} (‘accessibility tables’) R package, which makes use of {openxlsx} for programmatic spreadsheet creation. The interface to {a11ytables} is simple so that analysts can concentrate on generating their statistical tables and leave it to the package to generate compliant spreadsheets that can be used by all citizens. The package is openly available on GitHub for anyone to use or contribute to, and has already been used to help create reproducible and accessible statistical publications for GOV.UK with minimal effort. In this talk I’ll discuss the package’s inception, development, design, features and future. Resource links can be found on the NHS-R Community website:
collection: NHS-OA Community: Webinar and Talk Recordings

title: NHS-R February 2023 Webinar: Introduction to Causal Inference and propensity modelling
details: Introduction to Causal Inference and propensity modelling Wednesday 15th February 2023 With Christel Swift, Principal Data Scientist, BBC About the webinar: In an ideal world, when trying to assess the effectiveness of a treatment (e.g. a new medicine, a government policy, a marketing intervention), we would use a randomized controlled trial. Unfortunately this is often not possible or practical and we have to make do with “observational studies”. Directly comparing a treated vs a non-treated group can be problematic because the two groups may have very different profiles prior to being treated. For example, how would you evaluate the effectiveness of programme trailers that are played before a viewer gets to watch their selected programme? It’s important to control for factors that influence both treatment (e.g. being exposed to a trailer) and outcome (e.g. going on to watch the promoted programme) before drawing any conclusion. This is what Causal Inference is all about. Add to that the computational challenge of dealing with large datasets and some methods may be suitable than others. This webinar will walk you through some key concepts of Causal Inference, including counterfactuals, causal graphs, propensity modelling, inverse probability weights, love plots, and marginal structural models. Resource links to text books, articles and online courses can be found on the NHS-R Community website

title: April 2023 Webinar: Introduction to Quarto for R Users
details: Introduction to Quarto for R Users Friday 21st April 2023 With Filippo Cavallari, Data Science Lecturer at The Office for National Statistics (ONS) About the webinar: If you are an R user, then you’ve probably been using R Markdown. And probably you loved R also because of R Markdown. But since July 2022 there is a new publishing system that you can use. It’s name is Quarto. What’s the difference? First, unlike R Markdown, Quarto is not a package, but it is a stand alone application. Therefore you can use it outside the R world, for example with Python or Julia. So it can support you better if you or your team are using more than one language. Also, if your preferred IDE is not RStudio, then you’ll find that Quarto works well also with VS Code, Jupyter, Neovim or any other text editor. And there is already plenty of guidance for all of this. For the perspective of R Users, Quarto solves some problems and adds new functionalities. R Markdown users will find that they won’t need to install additional packages for specific publications (like Bookdown for books, Blogdown for websites and blogs, Xaringan for slideshows). Moreover Quarto keeps the syntax consistent in all publishing formats. This webinar will present some of the new functionalities of Quarto, highlight few but important syntax differences with R Markdown, and cover some tips and tricks Filippo learned using Quarto during the past year. title: How to turn your hospital's EHR data into predictions of emergency demand for beds
details: In this first of two webinars, I will provide detail on how to do this modelling including what our users (bed managers) wanted and how we catered to their needs • what data you need to do this modelling in your hospital • what data structures are suitable for prediction of short-term demand and how to transform EHR data into these structures • a high-level introduction to the modelling steps applied to the data • how we made our demand predictions aspirational (to reflect ED 4 hour targets) • how we evaluated model performance This webinar is intended for • any analyst or data scientist who works with EHR data (it does not matter which EHR your hospital has), or is interested in doing so • students of health data science and/or operational research • anyone with interest in using the predictions from such models to support patient flow, including operational managers and academics A companion webinar will show how this modelling is done in Python, including an introduction to the Python package we are developing for modelling patient flow. title: May 2025 Webinar: Surfacing the weekly consequences of ED admission delays by statistical modelling
details: Surfacing the weekly consequences of ED admission delays by statistical modelling implemented within an automated ML pipeline Wednesday 14th May 2025 With Dr Richard Wood and Dr Nick Howlett Content Summary: Surfacing the weekly consequences of ED admission delays by statistical modelling implemented within an automated ML pipeline A statistical analysis on three years of BNSSG data has quantified the extent to which delays to admission from ED are associated with poorer patient outcomes and knock-on impacts to the wider ED and, in turn, to ambulance handover and response times. Following this analysis (published here: the models have been implemented on weekly ECDS data to estimate the magnitude of these consequences, with results being refreshed each week and displayed through an R Shiny app hosted on a Linux server and accessible to the wider ICS. It is hard to know how to intervene when the extent of a problem is unknown, and so it is hoped that surfacing these impacts will provide a valuable first step in helping to properly illustrate the true scale of the problem.

title: August 2025 Webinar: An Improved I Chart
details: An Improved I Chart Wednesday 13th August 2025 With Dr Jacob Anhøj and Professor Mohammed A. Mohammed Content Summary: A webinar on simplifying statistical process control with I-prime charts In this webinar, we introduce the I-prime (I') chart – a new SPC tool that retains the simplicity of the I chart while addressing its limitations. It handles both measurement and count data, adapts to varying subgroup sizes, and holds the potential to replace other common SPC charts. Target audience: The webinar is intended for analysts and practitioners involved in healthcare quality control and improvement. Prior experience with SPC methodology and programming in R will be beneficial. Preparations and materials: No preparation is required to participate in the webinar. However, if you would like to refresh your understanding of basic SPC theory and practice, we recommend browsing Part 1 of our work-in-progress book: • Anhøj & Mohammed (2025): Mastering Statistical Process Control Charts in Healthcare. A book under development. If you want a head start on the theory behind I' charts, we recommend reading Taylor's original paper: • Taylor (2018): Normalized Individuals Control Chart. The original article introducing I' charts. • A free e-book: Mohammed MA. Statistical process control. Cambridge University Press; 2024 Feb.

details: Breaking it up: an approach to reproducible analytical pipelines (RAPs) Thursday 11th December 2025 With Georgina Anderson Content Summary: Writing a piece of code that can be re-used is a great thing, but how can we optimise our code to facilitate reproducibility and re-usability? My talk will cover the benefits of using a modular structure for RAP code, based on the principle of breaking tasks down into manageable chunks to facilitate development, maintenance, readability and re-usability. The session aims to challenge how developers think about their code and explain why it’s important to think beyond delivering the end product from the start.

title: September Webinar 2025: Complexity Made Approachable: Rethinking R-Based Modelling for Healthcare
details: Complexity Made Approachable: Rethinking R-Based Modelling for Healthcare with AM-Smart Tools Thursday 11th September 2025 With Brian Castellani, Corey Schimpf and Chris Caden Content Summary: The rapid rise of data science and its wide array of computational methods has widened the gap between those creating the methods and those able to use them. In response, we developed COMPLEX-IT, a case-based modelling platform built in R and Shiny, designed to make advanced computational techniques – clustering and self-organizing maps, systems mapping – approachable for those traditionally excluded from such methods, including policy analysts, applied researchers, and public sector practitioners. COMPLEX-IT is a prototype of what we call AM-Smart: Approachable Modelling and Smart Methods, a new methodological genre grounded in the learning sciences, human-computer interaction, and the epistemology of complexity. AM-Smart platforms follow nine design principles: bespoke method focus, integrated suites, embedded expertise, scaffolding, formative feedback, visual reasoning, productive failure, user-driven inquiry, and methodological rigor. Using modular R packages and Shiny’s interface logic, we engineered COMPLEX-IT to scaffold complex reasoning without sacrificing integrity. Along the way, we learned a lot about how to balance flexibility and simplicity, and how to build tools that support both learning and serious analysis. We’ll walk through our development process and invite others in the R community to build on this work, especially those interested in applied modelling and user-friendly design.

title: PatientFlow: python package for predicting short-term demand for emergency beds | Dr Zella King
details: (Part 1) How to turn your EHR data into predictions of emergency demand: Code: University College London Hospital (UCLH) has a real-time application predicting short-term emergency demand for beds that is now in daily use by bed managers. The work has attracted wide interest among trusts and ICBs who are keen to anticipate and manage pressures on hospital capacity. Dr Zella King, Health Data Scientist in the Clinical Operational Research Unit at UCL is the lead researcher on this work. In this webinar, she shows an example of how to do this modelling in Python including: - an overview of the patientflow repository on GitHub, which contains all the modelling code used at UCLH, as a Reproducible Analytic Pipeline - the datasets that have been made available by UCLH, which are derived from Electronic Health Record (EHR) data and based on real ED visits - a walkthrough of some Jupyter notebooks showing the modelling steps. These include (a) use of a XGBoost classifier to predict patient-level probability of admission after ED (b) aggregation from patient level predictions of admission to bed counts by specialty of admission (c) modelling of admissions within a prediction window from later arrivals (d) how to make the modelling aspirational, by assuming the ED meets its targets Project Team: Dr Zella King, Clinical Operational Research Unit (CORU), UCL (zella.king@ucl.ac.uk) Jon Gillham, Institute of Health Informatics, UCL Professor Sonya Crowe, CORU Professor Martin Utley, CORU Bio: Zella King is a health data scientist in the Clinical Operational Research Unit (CORU) at University College London. She applies data analytics, machine learning, programming and organisational psychology as tools for better decision making in healthcare operations. She is currently an embedded researcher at University College London Hospital (UCLH), where develops analytical tools that help the hospital anticipate and respond to short-term capacity pressures. Zella developed a real-time application that is in daily use by the patient flow team at UCLH to predict demand for emergency beds, and is lead author on a paper about this work that has been published in Nature Digital Medicine. Her team at UCL won a London Higher Healthcare Partnership of the Year award for their work with UCLH, and were finalists for a HSJ Digital award in Improving Urgent and Emergency Care. Zella gained her PhD in Organisational Psychology from Birkbeck College. Her academic career began with 15 years in business schools. Her work on human resources, careers and networks has been published in top business journals. In 2016, concerned about healthcare in ageing societies, she changed fields to focus on health data research. She gained a distinction in UCL's MSc in Health Data Science and was recognised in the Dean’s List for outstanding students in 2020-21.

title: Understanding Functions in R
details: This is an introductory-level workshop aimed at analysts who can write R code but who don’t really get what functions are yet. We’ll be turning some repetitive code into functions, and learning: – how to make a function; – what makes functions useful for analysts. I coded for ages before I understood what the point of functions was. And then I went through the torment of trying to learn how to use them! Now I use them all the time and I would never go back. This workshop will explain why, and you’ll be learning through doing. Pre-requisites: you are someone who can write at least some basic R code. To play along, you will need to have R, and RStudio or VSCode, installed and working on your computer. Ideally you will also be able to clone a GitHub repository into an RStudio project.

title: NHS-R Workshop: Interactive Visualisations for Beginners in Python with Shiny Apps
details: Interactive Visualisations for Beginners in Python with Shiny Apps Thursday 07th December 2023 with Dr Pawel Orzechowski 10:00am until 12:00pm (UK time) Course Description: Imagine coding an interactive demo and sharing it with the world within minutes. Your data could be displayed as maps or graphs, which change in response to sliders or dropdown menus. On this basic course we will make a jump from coding simple static graphs to being able to share interactive, visual and publicly available digital experiences. At last, you’ll be able to set your graphs free and share them with your collaborators, participants and funders. During the workshop we will build a web application using Shiny Python. Our Full-Stack app (with server, client and data layers) will be written in Python (without HTML or javascript) but will be exported as an interactive online dashboard. This class is suitable to both advanced and beginner coders (so a basic understanding of Python or R is required). During this interactive workshop you will collaborate with each other using pair programming (you will need camera and microphone) and we will code in an online interface, so no pre-installed software is required.

title: Introduction to R and R Studio Part 1 with Annie Yu on 21 February 2024
details: Learn about how to import data, wrangle data and produce and export graphs. Pre-requisites: No prior knowledge of R is required; however, it is assumed that you will have a moderate level of computer literacy. For example, you will be able to navigate to drives and files and be confident in searching for solutions to technical problems on the internet. You will work with, or have an interest in, data. About the course: This is a great opportunity for anyone who is interested in data analysis using Excel, SQL, Access or uses statistical programmes like SPSS to get started with R and R Studio. After this course, you will: See examples of R in producing healthcare related visualisations and use publicly available healthcare data to answer questions. Recognise and understand key terms often used by users of R. Interact with R using the RStudio environment. Learn how to set up some of the accessibility features of RStudio. Take charge of their workflow using RStudio projects. Import data into R using csv files (other data sources will be discussed). Carry out data manipulation using simple steps to solve complex problems. Join multiple tables together. Produce and save plots using ggplot2. title: Midlands Analyst Huddle: Exploring analysis of primary care services, Steven Wyatt - 24/02/2022
details: Steven Wyatt - exploring analysis of primary care services Steven Wyatt, Head of Research and Policy at the SU, discusses analysis of primary care services. ICSs will soon be assuming responsibility for commissioning GP services. Although 10% of the NHS budget is allocated to primary care, novel analyses of the service are few and far between. Analysts often say that data access is the key constraint. This session explores opportunities to improve and extend analysis of primary care services. Summary: In the first half of the session, we will be describing summary primary care datasets that are available from public domain websites. Have we made the most of these datasets? We will be assessing network member interest in collaborating on projects that use these datasets. In the second half of the session, we will be discussing record-level primary care datasets: proposed national data flows, research datasets and local solutions.

title: Midlands Analyst Huddle: A Data Visualisation Taster, Dan Isaacs - 13/01/2022
details: A Data Visualisation Taster: How to Communicate Effectively with your Data We have Dan Isaac who is going to be giving us a taster session for the 1-day course Dan delivers on Data Visualisation. Creating effective data visualisations is no longer a task for highly technical specialists and design professionals. In the modern workplace, we are all responsible for the data that we produce and learning how to effectively communicate with this data can be an invaluable asset. Drawing content from a full day workshop that Dan Isaac has been delivering through the Midlands Decision Support Network, this introductory session will provide a brief overview of some of the key psychological and practical principles of effective data visualisation “Your Data Viz session today was superb, and backed up by lots of valuable theory and practice. title: MAN Huddle: Federated analytics of linked health data in the UK  - Networked Data Lab - 24/03/2022
details: The Health Foundation present 'Federated analytics of linked health data in the UK – Introducing the Networked Data Lab' MAN Huddle with the Health Foundation’s Networked Data Lab – a UK-wide collaborative network of analytical teams across the UK working together to use linked datasets on the most pressing challenges facing health and care. Fiona Grimm (Senior Analytical Manager) and Sebastien Peytrignet (Senior Data Analyst) will take you through why and how the Networked Data Lab was set up, and discuss their approach to bringing local systems together to provide insights for local and national system leaders to take action to improve the UK’s health and care. title: MAN Huddle: New guidance for cross-system intelligence functions - 07/04/22
details: What does the new guidance for cross-system intelligence functions mean for me?' Find out more about what the new guidance for cross-system intelligence functions means for us as analysts in the Midlands. Each ICS in England is required to develop a ‘cross-system intelligence function’, as described in NHSE/I’s Integrating Care, the ICS Design Framework. The purpose of an intelligence function is to enable high quality decisions to be made. David Callaghan (the Strategy Unit) is going to be talking to us about the guidance and the supporting toolkit and sharing case studies to help us understand how the guidance affects us and how we can get involved.

details: ‘Impactibility’ from techno buzzword to action! With Andi Orlowski (Health Economics Unit) We are delighted to welcome Andi Orlowski (Health Economics Unit) who will be talking to us about Impactability and its role in Population Health Management. Risk stratification alone is often not enough – impactability modelling goes further to predict which of those high risk patients are most likely to respond to an intervention and suggests which changes to care are most likely to lead to better health outcomes. But not only that, we also have Jack Ettinger (Health Economics Unit) telling us about Allocative Efficiency and STAR (Socio-Technical Allocation of Resources) so this is a session not to be missed!

title: MAN Huddle: ‘Strategies to reduce inequalities in access to planned hospital procedures' - 05/05/22
details: Steven Wyatt (Head of Research and Policy, Strategy Unit) shares his strategies to reduce inequalities in access to planned hospital procedures (MDSN project) In last year’s report, ‘Socio-economic inequalities in access to planned hospital care: causes and consequences’, Steven Wyatt and Jake Parsons described how people living in more deprived areas have poorer access to planned hospital care than their more affluent counterparts. These deficits are widespread, substantial, and worsening. In his new report, Steven moves beyond describing and explaining the problem, providing practical support for those keen to address it. The Strategy Unit starts from the premise that inequities are not immutable. Tackling the issue will not be easy, but it is essential if the NHS is to be true to its founding principles. Efforts to date have clearly not been sufficient. Bolder action and more potent interventions are required. Steven will share with us his approach, key findings and look at how systems can implement the changes needed to reduce inequalities in access to planned hospital procedures.

title: MAN Huddle: Using system dynamics to gain insight into domiciliary care - 14/07/22
details: Title: Using system dynamics to gain insight into domiciliary care AND the launch of a new system dynamics development programme In the Huddle on 30/06/22 we had an introduction to System Dynamics and an example of how this was used to support capacity planning If you’d like to have a go, yourselves, then please do try out this System Dynamics ‘Ready Reckoner’ which is a simple model structure is to give an introductory insight into how System Dynamics is used to model capacity in health and social care services. This week’s Huddle is another look at System Dynamics – this time in relation to domiciliary care and we are also going to learn about an exciting opportunity for you as part of a new system dynamics development programme. The Strategy Unit and Douglas McKelvie have been working on an exciting project with WM ADASS, the Association of Directors of Adult Social Care Services in the West Midlands to explore the challenges facing domiciliary care and the opportunities that exist to transform and improve the service. If domiciliary care is not provided, then the effects are felt not just by those who need the service, but also by a wide range of aligned health and care services: hospital beds become blocked and care home beds are overrun. “Using system dynamics we have been collaborating with local authorities to develop through iteration a model which gives us a better grip on what the future might hold and how options to address future challenges might perform.” And in addition, we are going to be learning about the exciting new development programme and opportunities for analysts and others to be part of this. In the Autumn the Strategy Unit and Douglas McKelvie will be launching a system dynamics development programme, as well as the core programme there will also be the option of enhanced support for some of the ICSs in the region to be part of a pilot in parallel with NHSEI to use system dynamics to tackle system-wide capacity and demand challenges.

title: MAN Huddle: Associations between some household context factors & emergency hospital use - 28/07/22
details: 28th July 2022 – Latest analysis on the associations between some household context factors & emergency hospital use Richard Brine and Liz Crellin from the Health Foundation are going to be talking to us about two household context factors that the Improvement Analytics Unit have derived from national routine administrative health data. These are: . living alone, and . living in a two-person household with someone who is frail. They have developed the indicators as they believe they can provide important and useful information related to social context when understanding population health and care needs and could be potential proxies for caring responsibilities or risk factors for social isolation. The session will demonstrate: . how the context factors were derived using a pseudonymised Unique Property Reference Number (UPRN) variable contained in a minimised version of an NHS England and Improvement dataset, the Master Patient Index, and . the results of their analysis into whether these household context factors were associated with emergency hospital use (A&E attendances and emergency admissions) in people aged 65 and over (approximately 5m patients). They found that both factors were strongly associated with both higher A&E attendance and emergency hospital admission, even after adjusting for common predictors of emergency use (age, gender, ethnicity, geographic region, level of socio-economic deprivation, historical emergency hospital use, frailty indicators and a range of long-term conditions).

title: MAN Huddle: Introducing Data Hazards -  07/09/22
details: Introducing Data Hazards – how can analysts and data scientists use Data Hazards in our day to day work? This session is be run by Zoë Turner, data scientist in Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust. 08/09/22 If our profession of data analysts/data scientists in health and care is to be recognised for the power of good we can do then we must also be responsible for highlighting how our work can potentially cause harm; and that’s where Data Hazards can help to facilitate those discussions. The process of outlining Data Hazards was started by Natalie Zelenka and Nina Di Cara, who also run the Data Ethics Club, on their website which is open to contribution and released under an open licence to use. The hazards are visually depicted, like COSHH chemical hazards, and are a concise way of communicating and inviting opinions on projects. Whilst Natalie and Nina concentrated on the value of this to research, this short introduction in this week’s Huddle will attempt to show how analysts and data scientists can use the Data Hazards in our day to day work. Together we’ll consider a couple of case scenarios and discuss the benefits (or perhaps not!) of using something like Data Hazards labels regularly in our work. We’d be really interested to see what you think!

title: MAN Huddle: Understanding the ageing patterns of the population in NW London - 22/09/22
details: Understanding the ageing patterns of the population in NW London: A survival analysis Recent analysis has found that demand for health and social care may not necessarily increase in line with an ageing population. Because older people may stay healthy for longer, or they may experience milder health conditions. The Health Economics Unit, with support from the REAL Centre, investigated whether this was the case in North West London. In this Huddle we will cover: Theories on whether an ageing population leads to higher lifetime health and social care spending Introduction to Survival Analysis Methodology for the North West London analysis Results from our analysis Recommendations and caveats It would be useful but not essential to have some basic analytical skills to understand the technical elements of this huddle but everyone is very welcome! After this session, you’ll have a good understanding of survival analysis, recent literature and a case study on the use of survival analysis Your presenters will be Yihan Xu and Santosh Kumar (Health Economics Unit).

title: MAN Huddle: Health implications of reduced access to care during the COVID 19 - 20/10/22
details: MAN Huddle: 20/10/22 MDSN Regional Analysis: What are the health implications of reduced access to care during the COVID 19 pandemic? Project Lead, Paul Seamer (Strategy Unit) describes his approach and key findings for this important Midlands Decision Support Network (MDSN) Regional Analysis. The MDSN agrees an analytical work programme every year. This is an annual programme of 3 projects determined by the network steering group and is focused on agreed network priorities. What are the health implications of reduced access to care during the COVID 19 pandemic? Access to many forms of planned and unplanned healthcare reduced dramatically during the COVID-19 pandemic and associated lockdowns. The aims of this project were to investigate: - The effect on health outcomes of changes in healthcare utilisation during the COVID-19 pandemic - The actions available to health systems to mitigate these effects This was done by: - Exploring how the overall activity changed, by looking at the trends in activity levels for key services, for example, A&E visits, planned admissions, emergency admissions and primary care consultations - In-depth analysis of unplanned emergency care to look for differences in current patterns of morbidity compared with pre-Covid - A focused analysis of the impact of reduced access to care for diabetes patients - Reviewing the implications for health care systems and identifying strategies and interventions to help health systems mitigate the negative effects

title: MAN Huddle: INSIGHT 2022 The new Health Index - Midlands Focus - 01/12/22
details: MAN Huddle INSIGHT 2022: Sam Booth (ONS) takes us through the new Health Index – Midlands focus 1st December 2022 Sam Booth, Lead Researcher (Integrated Care Systems and Health Index) joins the Huddle to tell us about the new Health Index. Find out more about the Health Index and how it can support Integrated Care Systems (ICS) to achieve their purpose and maximising the impact of the index at a local level. The Health Index for England is a new measure of the health of the nation. It uses a broad definition of health, including: - health outcomes - health-related behaviours and personal circumstances - wider drivers of health that relate to the places where people live The Health Index: 2015 to 2020 provides a systematic, independent view of health in England. It can be used to compare health over time and across geographies. It gives a picture of health in its broadest sense, recognising the importance of health outcomes, risk factors and the social, economic, and environmental drivers which affect people’s lives. Data is published at local authority and integrated care system geographies as well as for regions and England as a whole. A semi-automated online article, how health has changed in your local area, presents users with data and insights for their local area. The session will cover: - What the Health Index is - Insights from the Health Index - How to access and use the Health Index at a local level - Next steps in development This Huddle will be of interest to policy makers, commissioners and analysts who aim to use data and insights about their populations to improve health now and for the long term.

title: MAN Huddle: Musculoskeletal patients experience of the OA hip pathway - A qualitative study 27/07/23
details: Midlands Analyst Huddle: Musculoskeletal patients' experiences of the OA hip pathway – A qualitative study. Supporting vulnerable patients and improving the management of long term conditions Date: 27/07/23 - What are the barriers and facilitators impacting on vulnerable patient populations? - How can we improve patient experiences and outcomes? In May 2021 the Strategy Unit produced an analysis of ‘Socio-economic inequalities in access to planned hospital care’, this reported on socio-economic inequalities in the levels of primary and secondary care treatments received by patients for four conditions: COPD, Heart Failure, Hip Arthritis (OA Hip) and Cataracts. In the Black Country the most prominent inequality centered on the OA Hip pathway, in particular in relation to levels of Total Hip Replacement surgery (THR). The Black Country Healthier Futures Academy set up a project, led by Rosalind Smithson (Principal Analyst – Qualitative Methods, Healthier Futures Academy, Black Country Integrated Care System) to explore patients’ experiences of the OA pathway, investigating what factors facilitated patients to gain appropriate support and what acted as a barrier. 15 in-depth interviews were conducted with patients at different stages in the pathway living in Sandwell or Walsall. Two focus groups were also conducted with First Contact Practitioners (FCP) and Advanced Physiotherapists on their experiences of working with patients and of the system itself. This session will give a brief overview of the Strategy Unit analysis (Steven Wyatt) before Rosalind Smithson’s presentation of the project findings and how these led to a series of applied pathway recommendations for improvement. The results focus on pathway navigation, and how the existing pathway relies on patients successfully negotiating the pathway largely on their own. In between touch points with medical professionals, patients had to manage their condition independently and co-ordinate the various aspects of their care. There were a number of system factors (e.g., the practice approach of health professionals, pathway processes, treatment criteria etc.,) which can support or create a barrier to patients directing and self-managing their condition, and patient factors (e.g., other health conditions, confidence, family support, etc.) that can support or act as a barrier.

title: MAN Huddle: Understanding Waiting List Pressures (using queuing theory) with Neil Walton - 02/11/23
details: MAN Huddle: 02/11/23 Understanding Waiting List Pressures (using queuing theory) With Neil Walton who is a Professor in Operations Management at Durham University Business School. Using queuing theory to understand the demand, queue size, waiting times, capacity requirements and trade-offs for different waiting lists. NHS waiting lists currently sit at record lengths due to a combination of the immediate impact of the pandemic and, as well as, long-run pressures requiring investment on NHS resources. These factors have left managers and clinicians with increasingly complex decisions when scheduling elective operations. It is imperative that managers understand the basic dynamics, tradeoffs, and pressures when managing waiting lists. Queueing theory is a key part of operational research, extensively used throughout manufacturing, retail, information technology and other sectors. This work provides an exposition of the theory of queues within the context of the current NHS backlog. With this information a manager will be able understand the demand, queue size, waiting times, capacity requirements and trade-offs for different waiting lists. We describe the metrics and a reporting system developed to understand waiting list pressures in a large NHS trust. Our aim is to enable managers to better understand their waiting lists, to achieve targets and improve health outcomes.

details: MAN Huddle: 30/11/23 Find the Future in You – The Health Service Modelling Associates Programme With Dr Daniel Chalk (HSMA Programme Lead) and Sammi Rosser (HSMA Trainer) In 2016, the Health Service Modelling Associates (HSMA) Programme ( was launched in South West England as a way to provide modelling and data science training and mentoring support to staff working in health and social care. Since its inception the programme has grown to a 15 month online programme open to anyone working in health, social care or policing anywhere in England free of charge. The programme is entirely open and teaches free and open source skills in Python programming, Discrete Event Simulation (pathway modelling), Geographic Modelling, Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, Agent Based Simulation, System Dynamics, Web Application Development and much more, and no prior knowledge of coding is required. Staff are released for a day a week from their usual role for 15 months to first undertake 6 months of training, and then supported by a community of over 300 modelling and data science experts to undertake a project that addresses an issue of importance for their organisation, immediately applying their new skills. Previous HSMA projects have led to £multi-million new mental health, support for the COVID mass vaccination programme, transformative improvements to urgent care services and the formation of dedicated modelling and data science teams within trusts. The programme has also become the first training programme accredited by AphA and offers certification for completion of the course. In this session, Dan and Sammi will talk in more detail about the programme, you’ll have a chance to speak with the programme staff and they will encourage you to attend their virtual HSMA Open Day on 13th December ( at which you can find out more about the programme and the application process, hear from current HSMAs about the work they’ve been doing, and sample mini-taster workshops that give you a flavour of HSMA teaching. title: MAN Huddle: 21/03/24 The 85% bed occupancy fallacy
details: MAN Huddle: 21/03/24 Topic: The 85% bed occupancy fallacy How useful is a bed occupancy target? With Nathan Proudlove, The University of Manchester This talk is in some ways a companion piece to Prof Neil Wilson’s talk on waiting list pressures, which used some insights from queuing theory models to consider the size of a bed pool required to keep the risk (or proportion) of patients breaching some waiting time limit within some target value (Fong et al, 2022). Analytical queuing theory models can give us quick, first-cut answers on a range of performance metrics, under certain conditions; more complex systems and contexts can be modelled (much more laboriously) by building computer simulations. A BMJ paper of a simple inpatient system (Bagust et al, 1999) was influential forming DH views on bed occupancy and management, but these were not well considered. In this talk we look at what queuing theory models tell us about the relationship between utilisation (e.g., bed occupancy) and waiting times, and reflect on the usefulness (or otherwise) of the policy of a target bed occupancy of e.g. 85%, as was prevalent in some DH guidance and trust policies some years ago. These models can give us further insights into things like the impact on performance of capacity carve out versus pooling (e.g., bed ring fencing vs pooling). The commonly used basic analytical queuing models (as above) require many assumptions for the maths to be tractable, including about the shape of the randomness in arrivals and service times (e.g. length of stay). This overlooks and hides the dramatic impact that the amount of variation (e.g., the standard deviation) has on system performance – and variation reduction is, of course, at the heart of improvement approaches such as lean an six sigma. The final stage is an approximate queuing theory model that allows us to see this impact of variation explicitly; in fact we can see that system Performance (e.g. expected waiting time) is related to Variation × Utilisation × service Time, the ‘VUT Relationship’. The size of the bed pool (i.e, the amount of bed pooling) is also an input to the model. So, with this we can see, and approximately quantify, the power of and trade-offs between these key drivers of system performance. The talk draws on material from Proudlove (2020) [also Proudlove (2023)]. Open access version of the paper: www.researchgate.net/publication/335487564_The_85_bed_occupancy_fallacy_The_use_misuse_and_insights_of_queuing_theory and its appendix: www.researchgate.net/publication/376678922_Proudlove_2020_HSMR_bed_occupancy_fallacy_App_17docx and Excel models: www.researchgate.net/publication/376678613_Bed_Pool_Calculator_30_SUBMITxlsx

To address this Chris Lee (Senior Information Analyst, Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust) developed a solution using SQL Server Integration Services (SSIS) , C# and T-SQL which is able to automatically back up SSRS reports which have been modified. This presentation will go over how to develop a system like this, how it works in practice and other potential uses of the same or similar code. The code that powers this solution will also be made available at the end of the presentation for anyone who would like to use it.

title: MAN Huddle: Forecasting in Retail and Healthcare – addressing common themes - 30/05/24
details: MAN Huddle: 30/05/24 Topic: Forecasting in Retail and Healthcare – addressing common themes With Dr Bahman Rostami-Tabar who is Professor of Data-Driven Decision Science, Cardiff University and Dr Stephan Kolassa, Data Science Expert In this session our presenters will address forecasting in retail and healthcare. They will focus on common themes across the two domains such as probabilistic forecasting, temporal granularity and forecast horizon, cross-sectional/hierarchical forecasting, and impact of special events. Stephan will look over the many retail processes that need forecasting and will dig a little deeper into his main focus areas, store and distribution centre replenishment and promotional planning. Bahman will discuss the use of forecasting in various areas of healthcare, and then investigate some cases including hourly forecasting in emergency departments (ED), daily forecasting in EDs with special events, hierarchical forecasting in ambulance services, long-term forecasting of ICU unit admissions, and mental health workforce planning. Who is this for? This session will be relevant to data analysts, modellers, professionals, or anyone interested in the development and application of forecasting techniques. What will you learn? 1. How forecasting methods apply to different domains such as retail and healthcare, highlighting the needs of each and common challenges. 2. Get insights into the use of probabilistic approaches that account for uncertainty in forecasts. 3. Learn about how to build forecasting models over different time frames, from hourly to long-term. 4. Find out more about approaches to integrate data across various levels of aggregation, from individual locations, and attributes to national. 5. Learn about strategies for integrating the impact of special events into models. 6. And learn about cases from each sector, giving examples of how to develop forecasting models.

title: MAN Huddle: How much healthcare will our population need in 5, 10, 20 years’ time? - 13/06/24
details: MAN Huddle: 13/06/24 Topic: How much healthcare will our population need in 5, 10, 20 years’ time? With Paul Seamer (Strategy Unit) How much healthcare will our population need in 5, 10, 20 years’ time? This is a staggeringly difficult question. By definition, the future is uncertain. And planning healthcare means making judgments about factors such as population size, age and healthiness – as well as how likely needs will differ for different services. This session will explore some of the challenges in modelling the impact of demographic change on future demand for healthcare. In particular, how to handle potential changes in population health status. Will 60 really become the new 50 or are we destined to spend more time living with chronic disease and disability? There will be a demonstration of a new interactive tool developed by the Strategy Unit with the aim of showing how population aging, and other demographic changes will impact the future need for different types of hospital services in your local area. The development of a web-based application is a departure from more traditional report-type outputs. To test the tools ease-of-use and to identify and remedy issues there will be an opportunity for attendees to volunteer to help with usability testing.

title: MAN Huddle: Describing general practice staffing mix using latent profile analysis - 27/06/24
details: MAN Huddle: 27/06/24 Topic: Describing general practice staffing mix using latent profile analysis With Alex Lawless, The Health Foundation General practices in England are currently facing major workforce pressures and rising demand for services. There is interest in understanding whether skill mix changes have improved access to general practice, increased the range of general practice services available to patients, or reduced use of other parts of the health care system. This analysis aims to identify clusters in practice staffing levels using routine general practice consultations and to assess distribution of clusters within practice deprivation quintiles. This cross-sectional study utilises Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) data to derive practice-level daily full time equivalent (FTE) rate per 1000 registered patients by staff group. Practice FTE rates by staff group were analysed using Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) methods to identify clustering. Practice Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) quintile and geographic region was linked to examine the relationship between demographic variables and practice staffing configurations.

title: MAN Huddle: 08/08/24 Health inequalities in 2040: Current and future patterns in England
details: MAN Huddle: 08/08/24 Topic: Health inequalities in 2040: Current and future patterns of inequalities in illness in England With Ann Raymond, The Health Foundation On current trends, health inequalities are projected to persist into the future. This has significant implications not just for population health but for labour supply and wider economic growth. The existence of wide inequalities in health across England is well-documented. This Health Foundation research adds to this evidence on inequalities in self-reported health by describing current patterns and projecting future patterns of inequality in diagnosed illness across multiple conditions by deprivation. They used the IMPACTNCD microsimulation model that simulates a close-to-reality synthetic population of adults in England from 2019 to 2040. This model combines individual-level data on demographics, health and mortality from linked administrative data for primary and secondary care with survey responses on individual-level risk factors and epidemiological evidence on the associations between risk factors and chronic illness. Ann and colleagues used the Cambridge Multimorbidity Score (CMS) as our multimorbidity measure. This assigns a weight to 20 common long-term conditions based on individuals’ healthcare use and their likelihood of death. We further focus on “major illness” which corresponds to a CMS greater than 1.5. In preliminary results, health inequalities are not projected to improve between 2019 and 2040. In 2019, the share of working age people living with major illness in the most deprived 10% of areas in England (14.6%) was more than double the rate seen in the least deprived 10% of areas (6.3%). In 2040, we project these rates to remain largely unchanged at 15.2% (13.0%, 17.6%) and 6.8% (5.4%, 9.1%) respectively.

title: MAN Huddle: NHSquicker: Shaping Demand for Urgent Care Using Real-Time Data  - 31/10/24
details: MAN Huddle: 31/10/24 Topic: NHSquicker: Shaping Demand for Urgent Care Using Real-Time Data and Digital Nudges With Nav Mustafee, Professor of Operations Management and Analytics at the University of Exeter Business School This research and impact work investigates whether indirect suggestions (nudges) can support patients needing urgent care to make more informed decisions about available healthcare choices. A nudge can be delivered using targeted adverts, mail campaigns, and, central to the theme of this research, through "digital" means using apps and wearables. NHSquicker is a platform co-developed with the NHS Trusts in southwest England. It is designed to deliver nudges to inform patients of alternative locations for urgent care. NHSquicker comprises: (a) a user-facing app that provides suggestions taking into account the live waiting time from Accident & Emergency (A&E) departments and Urgent Care Centres (UCC)/Minor Injury Units (MIU)/Walk-in Centres (WICs), also factoring the travel time; (b) the platform backend that receives real-time feeds and allows for easy integration of new feeds from Trusts that join the initiative. The app helps patients make informed decisions, for example, whether they visit a facility which may be nearer to them but with a long waiting time or travel to an alternative location that is further away but with a shorter waiting time. An evaluation framework captures evidence of impact and triangulate findings from patient questionnaires, secondary data analysis and app analytics. Our study has shown the potential of NHSquicker to shape demand for urgent care by reducing A&E visits from low-acuity attendees and helping redirect patients to UCC/MIU/WICs and other healthcare facilities. A sustained communication effort by the NHS will further increase patients' adoption of NHSquicker (or other such real-time solutions) and help realise further benefits for the Trusts. The NHSquicker project was initiated in 2017 at the University of Exeter Business School. Over the years, the network has grown. It currently covers all urgent care facilities in Devon, Cornwall and Somerset. It received funding from NHS Devon ICB in September 2023. Meet our presenter: Navonil (Nav) Mustafee is a Professor of Operations Management and Analytics at the University of Exeter Business School. His research focuses on Modelling & Simulation methodologies and their application in Healthcare Operations Management, Supply Chain, Sustainability and the Circular Economy. Nav is the joint editor-in-chief of the Journal of Simulation (UK OR Society journal) and associate editor of Health Systems and Simulation: The Transactions of the SCS.

details: MAN Huddle: 12/12/24 Topic: COMPLEX-IT: Enabling Non-Experts to Leverage Advanced Computational Modelling for Policy Evaluation and Decision Making With Brian Castellani, PhD. FAcSS, Professor of Social and Public Health, Director, Research Methods Centre, Co-Director, Wolfson Research Institute for Health and Wellbeing, Durham University, UK; Adjunct Professor of Psychiatry, Northeastern Ohio Medical University, US and Lasse Gerrits, Professor and Academic Director, Institute for Housing and Urban Development Studies, Erasmus University Rotterdam, the Netherlands Over the past decade, computational methods for decision support - ranging from simulation and machine learning to network analysis and systems mapping—have advanced significantly. However, the challenge remains in making these tools accessible to non-experts, particularly those involved in healthcare research, strategy, and policy evaluation. This methods session addresses that need. Brian introduces COMPLEX-IT, a free, intuitive R-platform designed to equip non-experts with cutting-edge tools in machine learning, data visualization, participatory systems mapping, network analysis, simulation, data forecasting, and cluster analysis. Through hands-on exploration of a real-world dataset, participants will gain a step-by-step understanding of how to use COMPLEX-IT to enhance decision making in healthcare. By the session’s conclusion, attendees will leave with a powerful, practical platform they can readily apply to their own research and policy evaluation efforts. For more, see This session is for anyone keen to learn more about how to use computational methods (e.g., AI, networks, simulation, systems mapping and machine learning) in their healthcare work or research.
