title: MAN: Public expenditure in the last year of life Nuffield Trust & Health Economics Unit - 20/02/2025
details: MAN Huddle: 20/02/2025 Topic: Public expenditure in the last year of life - Nuffield Trust & Health Economics Unit With Lisa Cummins and Gayathri Kumar, Health Economics Unit Supporting people at the end of life is a crucially important element of public spending, yet there is remarkably little evidence available on how much money is being spent on it, and what that money goes on. The Nuffield Trust and the Health Economics Unit were commissioned by Marie Curie to estimate the range of public expenditure that supports the care of people in their last year, to help inform national and local funding decisions to improve services for people at the end of life. • Around 650,000 adults die each year in the UK, with one in six dying in poverty. We know that the care and support people receive from publicly funded services greatly influences the quality of their last year of life – yet very little is known about the cost of the care and support they receive. • To address this gap, and to help inform decision makers on the best possible use of funding, the Health Economics Unit (HEU), in collaboration with the Nuffield Trust, were commissioned by Marie Curie to estimate how much the UK spends on people in the last year of life. "We undertook analysis of published data and statistics and extensive stakeholder engagement to estimate how much health care, social care and social security funding was spent on people in their last year of life across all four nations of the United Kingdom (UK) in 2022. We also performed sensitivity analysis to assess uncertainty in our estimates."

title: MAN Huddle: 03/04/2025 Toy Model for risk stratification and healthcare needs in the future
details: MAN Huddle: 03/04/2025 Topics: Toy models – Complex problems in small packages! and How much healthcare will our population need in five, ten, 20 years' time?” With Andy Hood and Lucy Morgan, and Paul Seamer, from the Strategy Unit Toy models – Complex problems in small packages! Often analysts find themselves in situations having to describe complex theories and their intended or unintended consequences to decision-makers but with data itself that is complicated or that overwhelms the theory. Toy models provide a way of distilling key mathematical concepts on a given topic or issue and providing simple data and a platform on which to explore, test and visualise them. The Strategy Unit (SU), funded through the New Hospitals Programme (NHP) is developing a series of toy models that explore risk stratification cost effectiveness, bed pooling & identifying bottle necks that impact patient flow and left-shift. These tools, it is hoped, will allow analysts, decision-makers, trainers and students to explore these concepts in a digestible way and gauge the high-level impacts of changing approaches before doing so at scale. In this bite-size session we will be introducing and demonstrating the Risk Stratification toy model app and trailing the other upcoming toy models which will all be made publicly available. Aimed predominantly at analysts, this session will (hopefully) introduce the key concepts in risk stratification implementation; demonstrate the impacts of changing any of these features; provide links to freely access this tool and describe plans for similar upcoming and future tools. 21:37 How much healthcare will our population need in five, ten, 20 years' time? At a previous huddle the Strategy Unit shared a beta version of a new interactive tool that showed how population aging, and other demographic changes will impact the future need for different types of hospital services across local areas. During the earlier huddle session, we asked for volunteers to help with usability testing. A number of people kindly volunteered to review the tool and provided helpful feedback. We are now ready to officially launch the tool. This short session will include a demo of the new tool, a reminder of the themes it addresses, and an opportunity to ask questions.

title: MAN Huddle: 'Rules of Thumb' for assessing the quality of analysis - 24/07/2025
details: MAN Huddle: 24/07/2025 Topic: 'Rules of Thumb' for assessing the quality of analysis With Fraser Battye (Strategy Unit) and Danielle Jefferies (The Kings Fund) How do you assess the quality of analytical work? When you first receive a report, what are the first signs and signals you are looking for? The author(s)? The layout? The methods? Data sources? Drafting? And - of all the quick tests of quality you are performing - could a non-analyst be primed to see the same things? Are there any 'rules of thumb' that non-analysts could use to assess the likely quality of analytical work? At this huddle, we will examine these questions with Fraser Battye (Head of Policy, Strategy Unit) and Danielle Jefferies (Analyst at the Kings Fund). They will present the results of a project, which drew on interviews with senior analysts, and suggest that there are pointers which non-analysts could use to get a first-approximation assessment of analytical quality.

title: MAN Huddle: Simplifying statistical process control with I-prime charts - 07/08/2025
details: MAN Huddle - 07/08/2025 Topic: Simplifying statistical process control with I-prime charts With In this Huddle, you will be introduced to the I-prime (I') chart – a new and improved SPC tool that retains the simplicity of the I chart while addressing its limitations. It handles both measurement and count data, adapts to varying subgroup sizes, and holds the potential to replace other common SPC charts. Target audience: The webinar is intended for analysts and practitioners involved in healthcare quality control and improvement. Prior experience with SPC methodology and programming in R will be beneficial but not essential. If this isn't you, you are still very welcome to come along and learn a bit more about SPC charts and about what can be achieved from programming in R. Aims: After the session you will: • understand the theory behind I' charts, • know when – and when not – to use I' charts as alternatives to traditional SPC charts, and • be able to construct I' charts using R. Preparations and materials: No preparation is required to participate in the webinar. However, if you would like to refresh your understanding of basic SPC theory and practice, we recommend browsing Part 1 of our work-in-progress book: • Anhøj & Mohammed (2025): Mastering Statistical Process Control Charts in Healthcare. A book under development. If you want a head start on the theory behind I' charts, we recommend reading Taylor's original paper: • Taylor (2018): Normalized Individuals Control Chart. The original article introducing I' charts. Also, you may wish to install and familiarise yourself with pbcharts, an R package currently in development: • Anhøj (2025): Process Behaviour Charts. Yet another R package for making SPC charts: devtools::install_github("anhoej/pbcharts")

details: MAN Huddle: 08/01/2026 Topic: From hospital to community: shifting care or swimming uphill? With Fraser Battye, Head of Policy at the Strategy Unit The shift from hospital to community is one of the three main aims of current health policy. This is not new. Indeed, the desire for a less hospital-centric health and care system has been a fairly consistent aim for several decades. Why has progress proved so elusive? details: MAN Huddle: 19/02/2026 Topic: Using data to inform the role of a specialist children's hospital in the left shift With Izaak Gilchrist. title: MAN: Building an open source model to understand future demand in CKD/KRT pathways - 05/03/2026
details: MAN Huddle: 05/03/2026 Topic: Building an open source model to understand future demand in CKD/KRT pathways with Strategy Unit colleagues In this session we will introduce our renal demand and capacity model (Kidney-SCOPE) and how we are developing it using the principles of open-science. Kidney-SCOPE is a hybrid simulation model for use in understanding the required capacity for renal services in the future under no-change and intervention scenarios. The model is novel in its use of system dynamics (SD) to represent the progression of (CKD) combined with the use of discrete event simulation (DES) to mimic patient pathways in kidney replacement therapy (KRT). The combination of models allows us to investigate the impact of interventions in both the upstream (i.e. prevention and new medications) and downstream (i.e. increase in home dialysis) models. Since October 2025 we have been redeveloping the original DES component of Kidney-SCOPE to make it available open-source using the simPy package in Python. We would like to use this session to reflect upon what we've learnt from the process and share what has and hasn't worked well. Disclaimer - we have now released version 1 of the model on GitHub but it is still under development as we receive feedback from the renal centres we're working with. What you will learn: • about hybrid simulation modelling for chronic conditions • the approach from commercial to open-source modelling Who is this session for? • Anyone with an interest in simulation, it won't be too technical so this should be of interest to a broad audience which could include commissioners, clinicians and any decision-makers who are interested in this topic • Anyone specifically interested in open-source modelling and inter-disciplinary working

title: MAN Huddle: The Art of the Adjacent Possible - 28/05/2026
details: MAN Huddle: 28/05/2026 Topic: The Art of the Adjacent Possible * With Neil Pettinger, Kurtosis During this Huddle Neil will explore if we can find data clues within existing practice that suggest improvements in patient flow might be more within our grasp than we think? Patient flow continues to be a problem for acute hospitals. And we are all aware that unless we can do something remarkable and sustainable to improve bed availability, it will continue to be a problem. But the directorates and specialties that manage hospital beds do not usually have ready access to data that would enable them to identify possibilities for improvement. This talk proposes a way of presenting flow metrics to inpatient directorates and specialties so that managers and clinicians can tap into the potential of internal benchmarking – what Neil is calling ‘the adjacent possible’* – in order to identify those possibilities for improvement. This is an exploratory session, and Neil will be actively inviting feedback on whether this approach feels credible, useful and workable in practice. * “What is actual now enables what is next possible: the adjacent possible.” -Stuart Kauffman

title: MAN Huddle: A deeper look at failure demand in healthcare - 11/06/26
details: MAN Huddle: 11/06/26 Topic: A deeper look at failure demand in healthcare With Alison Turner, Head of Knowledge Mobilisation, The Strategy Unit In this Huddle, Alison Turner, Head of Knowledge Mobilisation, will take a deeper, more analyst-focused look at failure demand in healthcare, following the broader Strategy Unit webinar on the same topic. Failure demand is the work created when people’s needs are not met effectively first time - for example, repeated contacts, avoidable follow-up activity, or demand generated by delays and fragmented care. One of the challenges is that this work can often appear in data as if it were productive output. Alison will introduce the key concepts, share an emerging typology of failure demand, and explore how analysts might begin to recognise it in their own datasets. The session will also reflect on the hidden costs for patients, carers and staff, and ask what it would mean to bring this perspective more explicitly into analytical work. This will be a reflective and participative session, with opportunities to test ideas and connect them to your own experience. Who is this session for? title: MAN Huddle: Do we need more hospital beds? - 06/08/2026
details: MAN Huddle: 06/08/2026 Topic: Do we need more hospital beds? With Lucy Morgan, Head of Analytics and Modelling at the Strategy Unit For more than 30 years, hospital admissions have risen while bed numbers have fallen. A major reason this has been possible is the remarkable reduction in average length of stay - from around 8.5 days in 1994 to approximately 2.6 days today. But length of stay is now levelling off and may be approaching its practical limit. If admissions continue to grow, what might this mean for future hospital capacity? In this Huddle I’m joined by, Lucy Morgan, Head of Analytics and Modelling at the Strategy Unit, who will introduce the interactive app Do we need more hospital beds? The app allows users to explore more than 30 years of national trends and test assumptions about admissions, length of stay, occupancy and future bed requirements. Lucy will show how it can be used to: • understand the trends that have shaped hospital capacity • examine how changes in admissions could affect future bed needs • explore how much activity different levels of bed capacity could support • test what may be reasonable to assume about future length of stay and occupancy • support better conversations about demand, capacity and hospital planning The model is deliberately simple, but it highlights an increasingly urgent challenge. If length of stay cannot continue to fall at the same rate, and hospital capacity cannot expand significantly, reducing growth in admissions becomes increasingly important. This session will be relevant to analysts, commissioners, hospital planners, clinicians, decision-makers and anyone interested in the future of hospital care. No specialist modelling knowledge is required.

title: MAN Huddle: Why Hospital Admission Avoidance Schemes May Not Reduce Bed Occupancy - 20/08/2026
details: MAN Huddle: - 20/08/2026 Topic: Hospital Admission Thresholds, the Left Shift, and Why Admission Avoidance Schemes May Not Reduce Bed Occupancy With Andrew Jones and Steven Wyatt, The Strategy Unit If admission avoidance and left shift successfully free up hospital beds… what stops those beds simply filling up again? Every patient attending an Emergency Department effectively encounters a threshold for admission. Clinical need is obviously central to that decision, but other factors can also play a part - including available hospital capacity and the alternatives to hospital care. So, if better community and neighbourhood services release hospital capacity, could the threshold for admission quietly fall? And if it does, might some of the capacity created through left shift simply be absorbed by patients who would previously not have been admitted? At the Huddle, I’ll be joined by my Strategy Unit colleagues Andrew Jones and Steven Wyatt, who have been exploring exactly this. They’ll explain the idea of an admission threshold, demystify casemix-adjusted odds of admission, show what they have found when looking at changes over time, and explore whether admission thresholds could potentially be monitored using routinely collected ED data. It should be a really interesting mix of analysis, methods and a much bigger question about how we make left shift work in practice.

title: Event 2 - What can we learn from the pandemic to reduce health inequalities?
details: The COVID pandemic has highlighted the stark inequalities in health that exist in the UK and globally. This session will reflect on some of the learning from the NHS frontline in Bradford and how data, science and community engagement was harnessed to protect a city. There is a second pandemic that is killing far more people than COVID - that of non-communicable disease. There are no simple vaccines or silver bullets for this pandemic. The solutions lie in tackling the wider determinants of health that interact in our complex social and urban systems. The session will describe one example of how a systems approach is being trialled that focuses on prevention rather than cures.

title: Festival Launch - new perspectives on analysis and decision making
details: Our Festival journey begins with the Strategy Unit team setting the scene on the importance of analytics, evaluation and evidence in addressing the current challenges facing health and care and supporting better decision-making – followed by two perspectives from our keynote speakers, Ben Goldacre and Andi Orlowski. Ben Goldacre will describe how open approaches can revolutionise health data science in the UK. Ben is a doctor, academic, writer, and broadcaster. He trained in medicine at Oxford and UCL, in psychiatry at the Maudsley, and in epidemiology at LSHTM. His academic and policy work is in informatics, epidemiology and evidence based medicine, where he works on various problems including variation in care, better uses of routinely collected electronic health data, evidence-based social policy, access to clinical trial data, efficient trial design, and retracted papers. His talk will explore key ways in which we can bring NHS data analysis into the 21st century and the value of ‘open by default’ approaches such as the OpenSAFELY analytics platform in advancing analytical collaboration across health and care. This will be followed by Andi Orlowski who will be exploring "Dangerous analytics…and how local analysts can save you!". Andi is a health economist and a national advisor for population health management (PHM). Andi starts his new role in October as Director of the Health Economics Unit at MLCSU, a new team working alongside and in collaboration with the Strategy Unit. His talk will include an exploration of the potential pitfalls and perils of analytics – the ways in which analysis can miss the point, can contribute to worsening inequalities and potentially cause harm. It will also highlight the value of working closely with local analysts to overcome these challenges and make better decisions. Both talks will be highly interactive and participants will have the opportunity to engage with two leading experts and gain insight into some of the latest perspectives on the use of analysis in health and care. The Strategy Unit’s Professor Mohammed A Mohammed will be on hand to host a Q&A with our speakers and to support the discussion. The session will close with a brief guide to navigating the festival and upcoming festival sessions. This session will be of interest to anyone who wants to see better use of analysis to support decision-making and we encourage all festival participants to take part in this opening session.

details: This session, hosted by the Strategy Unit, describes the development of the Decision Support Network and the importance of analytics, evaluation and evidence for addressing the current challenges faced by health and care in the region. title: Introduction by Peter Spilsbury, Director of the Strategy Unit
details: In this video Peter Spilsbury (Director, the Strategy Unit) introduces the Insight 2020 Festival, describing what it's all about and why we decided to do this. Week 1: Our decision-making context in 2020 Transformation in health and care has been rapid and intensive, particularly in 2020. Asking the right analytical questions requires joined-up approaches, between leaders and their analytical workforce, as well as broader system stakeholders. This week’s theme focused on the vital issues facing decision-makers, the contexts they are operating in, and from where they might draw support. Week 2: The role of the Decision Support Network The Midlands Decision Support Unit (DSU) Network is a new and emerging approach to bring together analytical resource across a region, develop analytical skills collectively and share learning from analytical projects. This week’s theme describes how the network will operate, shares some of the learning from systems who have adopted this approach already and describes how evidence will underpin the Network's approach to decision-making. Week 3: Analytical Priorities of the Decision Support Network The Midlands Decision Support Unit Network has defined its analytical priorities for 20/21. This week’s theme described the projects being carried out on behalf of the Network to respond to these priorities, the outputs they will produce and how these will be shared with the DSU Network and its partners. This included the presentation of work already completed on behalf of the Network, focusing on resource usage in the last two years of life. This week we also considered: what this way of working means for the future of analytics – what opportunities could it create for our analysts, our leaders and our population? Week 4: Exploring health inequalities COVID-19 has shone a light on health inequalities; it has “laid bare our longstanding social, economic and political inequalities…” (BMJ, 2020) and this is against a backdrop of declining life expectancy in our poorest communities, well before COVID-19. The Marmot review 10 years on found that regional and socioeconomic differences in health are large and growing. Michael Marmot describes this as ‘shocking’ and that we should work towards creating the conditions for everyone to be able to lead lives they have reason to value. During this week’s theme we shared a special selection of events which looked at health inequalities through very different lenses. We considered where health inequalities exist, what we have learned during the COVID-19 pandemic and what we are doing to address them that we need to amplify? Week 5: The Decision-making toolbox Decision-making is an art; we can train at it, rehearse and access tools to support us. However, humans are also subject to a wide range of biases which can undermine the quality of decision making, especially in complex real-world systems. This week’s theme focused on the range of materials that exist to help us be better decision-makers. We also thought about how we make best use of resources to collect the right evidence to support our decision-making, ensuring our methods are tested and reviewed with the aim of continuous improvement. Week 6: Making the most of our decision-making resources The final week’s theme was a reflection on what had been heard in the previous weeks. We thought about how we develop our analytical leaders by building on the success of the Midlands Population Health Management Academy and thought conceptually about ‘what makes a good decision?’, drawing on the tools and techniques shown over the course of the Festival. Concluded by an expert panel who considered where we go from here… Contact / links: The Strategy Unit Strategy Unit website: strategyunit.co.uk Twitter: @Strategy_Unit Insight 2020 Midlands Decision Support Centre website: Twitter: #Insight2020

title: Event 18 - Homelessness and Covid 19 using research to learn in a crisis
details: Context: Covid-19 brought crisis to many people already in crisis. For people experiencing homelessness it led to radical changes in circumstance, not least as the ‘everyone in’ policy changed their housing situation. Health and care services also had to make radical changes in their operation. This provided an opportunity to learn. Of these changes, which represented improvements on previous practice? Which were a step back? Which needed further evaluation? During this session we hear about the experiences of research teams from homelessness charity Groundswell and the Strategy Unit. Both had been asked to gather evidence to provide decision makers - in NHS England and NHS Improvement (NHSE/I), and elsewhere – with the insights they needed to learn from the health and care response to homelessness during COVID-19. title: Event 19 - The trauma impact of COVID 19 on children and young people - how to respond
details: Context: Whilst for children and young people the direct impact of COVID-19 has been limited, the impact of COVID-19 on family and society and the experience of lockdown have both been profound in their effects. It seems certain that many children and young people have experienced trauma as a result of the pandemic and our response to it. In addition, we know that children’s use of even urgent health services during COVID fell dramatically, with parents /guardians making difficult choices in the face of uncertainty about relative risks. The question of whether that represents a latent pool of harm or instead a falling away of demand that was ‘cautionary but not necessary’ is still to be properly answered. This session, "The Trauma of COVID-19 - a creative response to the effects of the pandemic and lockdown on children and young people" was an open exploration of the range of trauma that has been experienced, its possible implications and how we as a society/ suite of public services need to respond to that and be creative in so doing. Speakers: Dr. Ingrid Wolfe (Chair, Consultant in paediatrics and public health; Director, Institute for Women’s and Children’s Health, Kings Health Partners) Nigel Osborne (Composer, researcher and international aid worker, Sally Rowe (Executive Director of Children’s Services, Walsall Council), Swaran Singh (Professor of Social and Community Psychiatry, University of Warwick) and Peter Spilsbury (Director, The Strategy Unit) Contact / links: The Strategy Unit Strategy Unit website: strategyunit.co.uk Twitter: @Strategy_Unit Insight 2020 Twitter: Insight2020 Festival #Insight2020 Midlands Decision Support Centre website:

title: Event 24  - Insight 2020 and NHS-R: Why the NHS and care system should use R
details: Background R is free, it’s highly sharable and is backed up by a community of R users who love to help and apparently when you get the R bug – you’re hooked! There are so many examples of its potential and the opportunities to ultimately improve care and outcomes. But this doesn’t ‘just happen’ and the aim is to dramatically increase the use of R especially within the NHS but to realize the potential, to see the explosion in quality, shared analytics – we need many more people to understand why and how this can happen. We are on a bit of a mission to hugely increase the use of R because we think it’s that important! In this event we do our best to share the value of R and how it could help you, your organization and your patients or users. The session introduced R - the open source programming language that’s used widely in finance and academia and is now being used more and more in health and care. title: Neighbourhood INSIGHTS: What can the NHS learn from neighbourhood working in other policy areas?
details: Join the Strategy Unit for the next session in the Neighbourhood INSIGHTS series, exploring how evidence and analysis can support the shift from hospital to community. The NHS is developing its approach to neighbourhood working. Together with partners in other services and sectors, it is devising new ways of working, and new ways of relating with local communities. There is much to learn from practice elsewhere. And there is a long, rich tradition of neighbourhood working in other policy areas. Programmes such as Big Local, New Deal for Communities and Pride in Place; initiatives such as the Independent Commission on Neighbourhoods, and organisations like Local Trust. All act as potential sources of insight. In this session, James Plunkett, Kinship Works and author of End State, will reflect upon this practice, drawing out potential lessons for neighbourhood health. In doing so, he will also address the tricky and perennial question of ‘scaling up’ good practice.

title: The risks of risk stratification in neighbourhood health
details: Neighbourhoods INSIGHTS' Series -The risks of risk stratification in neighbourhood health The theory behind risk stratification is seductive. Almost irresistible in fact. It is that running algorithms over (mainly) primary care data will allow services to spot individual patients at high risk of unplanned hospital care. And then – by intervening early – that services can prevent poor outcomes. This has not worked in practice. Indeed, the reverse may be closer to the truth: evidence suggests that this use of risk stratification may even increase the use of unplanned care. So what has gone wrong? Where does this leave us? And what does this evidence mean for people planning and delivering neighbourhood health? This session, chaired by Fraser Battye, will present insights from Steven Wyatt (Strategy Unit), Jess Morley (Yale University) and Thea Stein (Nuffield Trust).

title: SU Insights   Downsides of Digital
details: This event in collaboration with the Health Foundation featuring Professor Trish Greenhalgh and experts explored the critical questions on the downsides of digital, drawing on research to reflect the implications of digital technology in health and care. There is widespread enthusiasm for the use of digital technology in health and care services, and shifting ‘from analogue to digital’ is one of the government’s priorities for the NHS. This shift promises significant gains in efficiency and productivity, and there are growing examples showing its potential in practice. But are we aware of the trade-offs that come with these advancements? Do we know what losses may accompany promised gains? Are there looming risks and downsides that need more attention? And what do we know already from the implementation of digital technologies? What lessons can be learnt? Event highlights include: Fresh perspectives on the risks of using digital technology in health and care. Insights into where digital technology can be helpful or harmful in health care. An overview of our recently published discussion document on the downsides of digital Presentations and discussions on the latest research, evidence and analysis. Key speakers: Fraser Battye, Head of Policy, Strategy Unit Trish Greenhalgh, Professor of Primary Care Health Sciences, University of Oxford Ellen Coughlan, Improvement Fellow, Health Foundation Ben Shemesh, Senior Improvement Analyst, Health Foundation Mahmoda Begum (Chair), Strategic Communications Lead, Strategy Unit

title: SU Insights - Contracting for Health Outcomes
details: The inaugural ‘SU Insights’ session explore the evolving landscape of "Contracting for health outcomes". The concept of outcomes-based commissioning was a hot topic in health policy around 15 years ago. Innovative contracting models were promoted as a way to transform the way services were paid for, to unleash innovation in delivery. But the reality fell short of expectations. Few schemes made it past the design stage. Of the few that did, many failed - often expensively. In this panel discussion leading experts explored the challenges and potential of outcomes-based commissioning in healthcare, why past efforts fell short, and what technical developments might help make these models more feasible today. Presented by the Strategy Unit, in collaboration with the Centre for Health Economics University of York, The Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS FT, NHS Confederation, and NHS England. Sign up here to be the first to hear about our next event:

title: Is ‘Do With’ the essence of neighbourhood health?
details: Event 3: Is ‘Do With’ the essence of neighbourhood health? Neighbourhood health is often discussed in terms of services: how they are structured, funded and delivered. But at its heart, it is about something more fundamental - relationships. In particular, the relationships between services and the people they support. A growing movement has emerged around this idea. Often described as ‘Do With’, it challenges traditional models of care that are designed ‘for’ people, or done ‘to’ people - instead advocating for approaches that are built with them. Is this the essence of neighbourhood health? If so, why does it matter? And what does it take to build and sustain more meaningful, community-centred relationships? This session explores: • What is meant by ‘Do With’ - and where this movement comes from • Why relationships are central to neighbourhood health • And how can richer service-citizen relationships be created and sustained? The session, chaired by Fraser Battye, will present insights from Dr Connie Junghans Minton (Imperial College London) and Adam Lent (Kings Fund). It will examine the intangible and important question of how services ‘Do With’, rather than, ‘Do To’ people.

details: NNHIP Evaluation and Analysis CoP: Drop in Sesssion NNHIP Care Shift Tracker - 04.03.26 In this Evaluation and Analysis Community of Practice drop-in session, there was and demo of a tool that is being developed to offer a system-wide view using a range of indicators to help spot emerging patterns, enablers and blockers relating to shifting care. The NNHIP Care Shift Tracker The challenge: Health and care systems, localities and communities are taking action to shift care away from hospitals where appropriate. Many of these actions are focussed on admissions avoidance, but in a complex and interdependent system, this alone will not be sufficient to shift care. Other activities and resource must also shift. What this tool offers: The Care Shift Tracker app offers a system-wide view of relevant indicators. Because no single metric can tell us whether care is shifting, this tool brings together indicators across acute, community, workforce and spend to help you spot emerging patterns - and understand what might be enabling or blocking progress. Helps to answers the questions:Is care shifting from hospital to other settings? What are the blockers and enablers? title: PART 2 Introduction to Discrete Event Simulation and SimPy - a Standalone Workshop (vidigi)
details: Part 2 of our two-part workshop. Discrete Event Simulation (DES) is a simulation modelling technique that allows us to tackle queuing problems in health and social care. These might include identifying delays in patient pathways and testing out the impact of reconfiguring processes and resources to try to reduce these delays. DES projects in the HSMA Programme have led to significant impact nationally, including the construction of an £11.8 million new mental health ward in Devon to allow patients in crisis to be seen closer to home ( transformative improvements to urgent care delivery in London ( and potential £1 million+ annual savings and improved patient outcomes for stroke patients in Kent ( In this special standalone workshop - developed for the NHS-OA community - participants will learn: - The principles of Discrete Event Simulation and the kinds of problems this modelling approach can be used to tackle - The importance of variability and stochasticity in simulation modelling - How to design reproducible stochastic models - How these models can be built in Python using the SimPy package, including how to use Python Generator Functions and how to structure code using Object Oriented Programming - How animated visualisations can be added to SimPy models using the vidigi package. Whilst participants should have some prior coding experience, this does not need to be in Python. We will assume no prior Python experience in this workshop. Instead, participants will be introduced to the components of a SimPy model and shown the code that write these elements in Python. Participants will also have a chance to adapt the code to write their own SimPy models. In addition, no local software installation of Python is required - instead, we will use Google CoLab as a way of writing and running code, which requires only a free Google account. The accompanying content for the workshop can be found here :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 7) 2A Introduction to Discrete Event Simulation
details: Today we begin module 2 of the programme, in which we explore how we can model pathway and queuing problems using a modelling method known as Discrete Event Simulation. We'll explore how Discrete Event Simulations work and you'll have a chance to design your own. GitHub (2A): Slides (2A): HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 7) 2B SimPy Part 1
details: Today we look at how we can use the SimPy Python package (which is built around generator functions) to build Discrete Event Simulations in Python. GitHub (2B): Slides (2B): HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 8) 2C SimPy Part 2
details: In this session we look at some more advanced DES concepts and how we can incorporate them in our SimPy models. This includes warm up periods, priority-based queuing, resource unavailability, Lognormal distributions, reneging, balking and jockeying. Slides : GitHub : HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 8) 3A Intro to Geospatial Problems in Health & Geographic Visualisation using QGIS Pt 1
details: In this session, we introduce some key concepts of geographic modelling and visualisation, and begin our exploration of the free and open source geographic visualisation software package QGIS. Slides : GitHub : HSMA Website :

(HSMA 6 Day 9) 3C - Visualising Travel Time Data in Python
(HSMA 6 Day 10) 3D - Location Allocation Problems
details: In this session we talk about how to construct and carry out the p-median location allocation problem - minimising a weighted cost across a region for different possible combinations of sites. Materials can be found here:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 10) 3C - A brief introduction to routingpy
details: In this video we briefly talk about the routingpy library and introduce how it could be used to retrieve travel matrices and isochrone data to assist in p-median location allocation problems and more. All materials for this session can be found here:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 10) 4A  - Introduction to AI and Machine Learning
details: In this session we introduce some of the core concepts of AI and Machine Learning, including the concepts of features and labels, overfitting and underfitting and assessing model performance. We also explore some of the different types of machine learning, and practice our understanding of these new concepts by seeing if we can unpick patterns in Dan's film preferences for "Dan's Desert Island DVDs". Slides : HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 11) 4B - Logistic Regression - Who Would Survive the Titanic?
details: In this session we'll begin exploring some of the Machine Learning approaches that we can use, starting today with Logistic Regression - a way of fusing together traditional linear regression models with a logistic function to create a powerful classifier model. You'll see how these models can be implemented in Python, and practice using both the Titanic dataset you saw earlier in the course, as well as a new stroke patient dataset. Slides : HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 11) 4C  - Ethics in AI
details: In this session we'll explore some of the key ethical considerations that are fundamental to any machine learning work, as we explore what can (and will) go wrong. Slides : HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 12) 4D Part 1/2 - Decision Trees
details: In this session we'll begin looking at how decision trees are built and how we can use the sklearn implementation of decision trees on our own datasets. We also recap sensitivity (recall), specificity and precision and how to calculate these in sklearn. Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 12) 4D Part 2/2 - Random Forests, F1 score + Confusion Matrices
details: In this session we'll take a look at how we can avoid some of the problems of decision trees by using an ensemble method - random forests. We also find out an easier way of calculating sensitivity, specificity and precision in one function, as well as hearing about a new metric called f1 score, and we learn about the confusion matrix, which is a powerful tool for helping to break down how different models perform. Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 12) 4E Part 1/2 - Boosting Trees for Classification Problems
details: In this session we'll take a look at a family of models called boosted trees. These are a very powerful type of algorithm that perform extremely well on tabular datasets. The session touches on XGBoost, AdaBoost, CatBoost, Histogram-based gradient boosting classifiers and LightGBM. Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 12) 4E Part 2/2 - Predicting Numeric Values with Tree-based Algorithms + OneHot encoding
details: In this session we take a look at how decision trees, random forests and boosted trees can also be used when you want to predict a numeric value instead of classifying a sample as a member of one group or another. We also touch on some key parts of data preprocessing so we can work with a new dataset of patient length of stay in the final exercise, covering how to OneHot encode categorical variables to make this data usable with machine learning libraries. Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 13) 4F Neural Networks
details: In this session we'll be looking at a subfield of AI that has dominated many of the big advancements in AI over the last few years - Deep Learning - as we introduce Neural Networks. Then, this afternoon, Sammi will dive into the fascinating emerging world of explainable AI as a way to build understanding, confidence and trust in our machine learning models. Slides: Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 13) 4G Part 1/6 - An Introduction to Explainable AI + Correlation vs Causality
details: In this part of the Explainable AI session, we explore - why explainability is importantant in AI models - what we mean by explainability - the difference between correlation and causation Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 13) 4G Part 2/6 - Feature Importance in Logistic Regression & Odds/Log Odds/Probability
details: In this part of the Explainable AI session, we explore - how we can extract feature importance from a logistic regression model - how to interpret the coefficients from logistic regression models - the relationship between odds, log odds and probability Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 13) 4G Part 3/6 - Feature Importance with MDI + PFI
details: In this part of the Explainable AI session, we explore - feature importance for tree-based models with Mean Decrease in Importance (MDI) - model-agnostic feature importance with permutation feature importance (PFI) Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 13) 4G Part 4/6 - Partial Dependence Plots and Individual Conditional Expectation Plots
details: In this part of the Explainable AI session, we explore - the partial dependence plot (PDP) - the individual conditional expectation plot (ICE) - ways of enhancing these plots Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 12) 4G Part 5/6 - Explainable AI with SHAP
details: In this part of the Explainable AI session, we explore - what Shapley values are - how the shap library allows us to look at global and local feature importance - how to create and interpret different shap plots Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 12) 4G Part 6/6 - Prediction Uncertainty
details: In this part of the Explainable AI session, we explore - why calculating prediction uncertainty may be useful - how to calculate and show prediction uncertainty Slides : Repository: HSMA Website :

title: (HSMA 6 Day 13) 4H - Reinforcement Learning
details: In this session we take a look at Reinforcement Learning in a session that will be very different to any you've experienced thus far. Note that we'd recommend not looking at the slides until after the first time the reinforcement learning game is played manually. Slides: App Link: App Github Repository: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 13) 4I - Synthetic Data using SMOTE
details: In this session we take a look at synthetic data - how to create our own fake but realistic data when we want to augment an underrepresented class, or just use the data instead of our real data. Slides: Github Repository: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 14) 4J - Optimising ML: Imputation, Feature Engineering & Selection, Hyperparameters
details: **Unfortunately the first 5 minutes or so of the lecture was not recorded** Covering a range of ways to improve your model's performance, including: - Missing Data Imputation with SimpleImputer and IterativeImputer - Feature Selection with SequentialFeatureSelector (forward and backward selection) and SelectFromModel (feature importance selection with model coefficients or mean decrease in impurity) - Feature Engineering - Dataset Splits (train/test/validation, k-fold) - Dealing with Imbalanced Datasets with model parameters - Hyperparameter tuning with exhaustive gridsearch, randomised gridsearch, and the Optuna framework Additional areas in the slides, but not covered in the video, are: - ensemble models - sklearn pipelines - automatic model selection with the flaml library - model calibration curves (reliability plots) Slides: Code Slides Only: Github Repository: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 14) 5A - Introduction to Natural Language Processing (NLP)
details: In this session we'll begin Module 5 and our journey into Natural Language Processing. We'll look at some core concepts important for processing text data, and learn a few little neat things we can do with our data along the way, including wordclouds and a method for assessing the similarity of different bits of text. Slides: Repository: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 15) 5B - Named Entity Recognition
details: In this session we'll continue our journey into Natural Language Processing. Have you got named entities? Do you need them recognised? Then have we got the session for you! Our session on Named Entity Recognition will talk all about named entities, and recognition of them. Along the way we'll stop by Sesame Street and Fraggle Rock, talk about Transformers, Parsing, Grammar, POS Tagging and more. Slides: Repository: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 15) 5C - Sentiment Analysis
details: In this session we don our pirate outfits and sail to the Caribbean as we look for the secret of Sentiment Analysis and Text Classification. We'll fight dastardly pirates as well as a pirate that's already dead but just won't accept it. Slides: Repository: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 16) 5D - NLP Hackathon
details: In this session, HSMAs worked in groups to tackle a question of their choosing on some data of their choosing using Natural Language Processing techniques, undertaking miniature projects and practicing those all-important skills needed to tackle their own projects in Phase 2. The recording contains the brief for the day, as well as 10 presentations of project plans after the initial hour, and 10 presentations of project outputs at the end of the day. Slides: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 17) 6B - An Introduction to Agent-Based Simulation
details: In this session, we begin looking at Agent Based Simulation - a simulation modelling approach that allows us to capture individual level behaviours of actors in our system, and observe the emergent dynamics. We also take a look at Cellular Automata, and head to the Edge of Chaos. Slides: Repository: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 17) 6A - System Dynamics
details: In this session, we take a look at System Dynamics as a way of understanding whether there are inherent issues in the way our systems are structured. We use the online InsightMaker ( tool to create a quantitative system dynamics model. Slides: Repository: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 18) 6C - Agent-Based Simulation with MESA
details: In this session, we look at how we can use the excellent Python package MESA to help us build our own Agent Based Simulations, and we'll revisit our old friend Object Oriented Programming to help us do that. Slides: Github Repository: HSMA Website:

title: (HSMA 6 Day 19) 7A - Version Control with Git and Github in VSCode
details: Today we're going to be looking at the crucial importance of version control, and how we can use Git - a distributed version control system - to allow us to this. We'll also look at how we can use Git interaction with GitHub to publish and work with repositories hosted online. Git is both amazing and horrible. If you feel that this all seems odd today, and convoluted, you're not wrong. But it IS important. Slides: Github Repository: HSMA Website:

details: We kick off this session with a recap of the key Streamlit commands (though we'd recommend going through session 7B if you're new to Streamlit: before a bit of a blast from the past - returning to our discrete event simulation (DES) code of a walk-in clinic from module 2 and turning it into an app. We then move on to sidebars, run buttons, multi-page apps, theming (with inbuilt theming tools and custom CSS), data caching, partial reruns with st.fragment, session state to allow us to store data across pages and model runs, and deploying our apps to the cloud. We also have a look at using a Python script to interact with the command line and produce multiple outputs from a single Quarto file using different parameters. details: An introduction to programming in Python. title: HSMA 5 3A : Introduction to Discrete Event Simulation and 3B : SimPy for DES Part 1
details: In these sessions, we introduce the simulation modelling approach Discrete Event Simulation - a way of modelling queuing / pathway problems. We then show you how to use the Python package SimPy to build simple but effective Discrete Event Simulation models. We also talk about Python Generator Functions - a structure that is fundamental to SimPy. Note - these introductory sessions show you how to build simple SimPy models using a non-Object Oriented structure. However, viewers are strongly recommended to additionally view the subsequent lecture which will show you how to structure a SimPy model in an elegant Object Oriented framework. Accompanying lecture materials can be found here : Session 3A : Session 3B : More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE @drdanielchalk

title: HSMA 5 3C : SimPy for Discrete Event Simulation Pt 2 & 7A : Introduction to AI and Machine Learning
details: In the first part of the video (session 3C) we look at how we can make our SimPy models more elegant by structuring them in an Object-Oriented way. We also look at how we can model entities having different priorities in a queue so that we use priorities to determine the next entity to be seen, and we look at how we can model unavailability of resources. In the second part of the video (session 7A) we take out first tentative steps into the magical world of AI and Machine Learning. We introduce some of the core concepts in these fields, with a focus on Supervised Machine Learning. We then challenge our HSMAs to come up with an "algorithm" to determine the films Dan most enjoys, learning concepts such as features, labels, overfitting, underfitting, and performance metrics en route. Accompanying lecture materials can be found here : Session 3C : Session 7A : More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE @drdanielchalk

title: HSMA 5 7B : Ethics in AI and 7C : Machine Learning - Who Would Survive the Titanic?
details: In the first part of this video (7B) we discuss some of the important ethical considerations necessary when undertaking AI and Machine Learning projects. We talk about issues around representation in our data, transparency of our models as well as the severe consequences that can happen when our AI models go wrong. In the second part of this video (7C) we look at using the scikit-learn Python library to develop a simple Logistic Regression model to see if we can predict which passengers would survive the sinking of the Titanic. We also look at how we can ensure our feature values fall on a consistent scale, look at how stratified k-fold validation can help us to improve model performance and we also look at Receiver Operator Characteristic (ROC) curves as a means of both assessing the potential performance of our model, as well as helping us to identify classification thresholds that will yield higher performance. Accompanying lecture materials can be found here : Session 7B : Session 7C : More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE @drdanielchalk

title: HSMA 5 7D : Introduction to Neural Networks and 7E : Synthetic Data
details: In the first part of this video (7D), we talk about Deep Learning and the magical world of Neural Networks. These structures allow us to get high performance learning models for a wide range of problems, although they do come with a cost - that we lose a little bit in terms of model explainability (at least "out of the box"). In the second part of this video (7E), we question whether anything is real as we delve into the world of Synthetic Data - methods that allow us to create fake data that can be used either instead of real data, or to augment our data where we don't have enough examples for a particular classification for our machine learning model. We talk briefly about a few different approaches, but then work through the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) approach. Accompanying lecture materials can be found here : Session 7D : Session 7E : More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE

title: HSMA 5 8A : Intro to Natural Language Processing and 8B : Named Entity Recognition & Word Clouds
details: IMPORTANT NOTE - there is an error in the teaching in this video which has since been corrected. Specifically, some of the named entities that I suggested should have been picked up as named entities in Exercise 1 should not have been - "bread" and "milk" are not named entities as they are not identified with a proper name (unless we are referring to a particular brand of bread or milk). Similarly, whilst "Discrete Event Simulation" counts as a named entity (as it has a proper name), "bread making" and "cookery" would not count. Similarly, I have removed "woodwork" as an example in one of the teaching slides. The materials in the links below (including the exercise solutions) have been corrected. In the first part of this video (8A), we introduce Natural Language Processing as a means of automating the extraction of information from unstructured / free-text data. We talk about Named Entity Recognition in particular, and explore common NLP concepts such as POS-tagging and parsing. In the second part of this video (8B), we talk about how the FOSS Package SpaCy uses Transformers at its core. We discuss how Transformers work in a broad sense, and talk about concepts such as Attention and Context. We then go hands-on with SpaCy to undertake some Named Entity Recognition. We also demonstrate use of the WordCloud library for generating word clouds from our text data. Accompanying lecture materials can be found here : Session 8A : Session 8B : More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE

title: HSMA 5 8C : Sentiment Analysis and 6A : Cellular Automata
details: In the first part of this video (8C) we revisit our old friend Neural Networks to see if we can apply the same principles to automatically predict the sentiment of a piece of text. But because we're dealing with text data, we'll need to look at the concepts of Standardisation and Vectorisation to get our text data Neural Network-ready. We also look at using a handy Keras method that allows us to easily read in text files from different directories representing different classifications for our training. We also talk a little bit about the field of Aspect-Level Sentiment Analysis, and Noun Chunks. In the second part of this video (6A), we begin our journey into modelling behaviour by dipping our toes into the world of Cellular Automata - the purist distillation of Agent Based Simulation. We jump in our oscillating spaceships, take part in a battle from Star Wars, avoid getting eaten by a Pulsar and journey to the Edge of Chaos and back again as we discover that the answer to life, the universe and everything is perhaps not 42, but the pattern on the cone snail Conus textile. We also explore some potential application areas for this abstract modelling approach. Accompanying lecture materials can be found here : Session 8C : Session 6A : More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE

title: HSMA 5 6B : Agent Based Simulation using MESA
details: In this video, we walk through some code to develop a simple Agent Based Simulation to model the spread of a disease using the Python package MESA. We talk about the concepts of Agent Based Simulation and how it can be used to model behaviour. We then look at how MESA is structured, begin developing a simple model and see and how we can use MESA's server-based capabilities to visualise our models. Accompanying lecture materials can be found here : Session 6B : More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE

title: HSMA 5 6B Part 2 : BYOABS (Bring Your Own Agent Based Simulation)
details: In this short video which serves as a part 2 to session 6B, the HSMA teams present their proof-of-concept Agent Based Simulation models built using MESA, and Dan gets his festive hat to wish you all a Merry Christmas! More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE

title: HSMA 5 4B : System Dynamics and 2C : Patient and Public Involvement in Research
details: In the first part of this video (4B), we introduce you to the world of System Dynamics. We look at how we can explore the influential dynamics within a system to try and understand something more about how the system works, and whether there are intrinsic problems within the structure of a system. We use a lovely online piece of software called InsightMaker to do this - it's completely free and just requires you to register for a free account. And the good news for those who need a break from coding - there's no Python (or any other language) needed, it's all drag and drop! In the second part of this video (2C), our guest lecturers Georgia Jenkins, Lauren Asare and Leon Farmer talk about Patient and Public Involvement in Research - what it is, why it's important and the practicalities of involving patients and public in your research. Accompanying lecture materials can be found here : Session 4B : More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE

HSMA 5 7F : Reinforcement Learning
details: In this video, we introduce some of the core concepts of Reinforcement Learning by using the 80s cult-classic UK TV series Treasure Hunt as our inspiration. We talk about the fundamental principles of Reinforcement Learning, the exploration / exploitation dilemma, multi-armed bandit problems and a Linear Operator Learning Rule. We also touch on Deep Q Reinforcement Learning as an extension to the core principles which incorporates Neural Networks, and take some time to think about potential application areas for these methods. title: HSMA 5 2B : Principles of FOSS and Version Control using Git
details: In this video, we introduce viewers to the world of version control using Git and collaborative open source development using GitHub. First, we talk about the importance of FOSS and Open Science. We talk a bit about the history of FOSS, as well as reminisce about the good old days of computing, when a "high resolution display" meant that you tuned your TV into a slightly less fuzzy picture. Then we move onto the meat of the session - introducing you to version control, and specifically, Git. We'll talk about why version control is so important using an example from Father Ted, and show you the basics of Git, before giving you a chance to have a go at using Git yourselves. Finally we explore the world of GitHub as an online sharing and repository platform, and how Git integrates with GitHub. You'll have a chance to play with Git integration with GitHub, and hear a funny story about what happened when I wrote this training. We draw our inspiration for the GitHub training from The Chuckle Brothers. Accompanying lecture materials can be found here : Session 2B : More information about the HSMA Programme can be found here : Follow us on Twitter : @PenCHORD_UoE

title: Introduction to Anaconda environments
details: An introduction to Anaconda environments, installing packages from conda, conda-forge and pypi (pip), and saving/loading environments. Create empty environment (called temp_env here): conda create -n temp_env Create environment with given Python version (just use python alone for latest available version): conda create -n temp_env python=3.7 Activate environment (before launching Spyder or Jupyter-Lab): conda activate temp_env Deactivate environment: conda deactivate List packages in environment conda list List environments: conda env list After activation environment install packages with conda, e.g. conda install jupyterlab spyder numpy pandas matplotlib scikit-learn Or install from Conda Forge: conda install -c conda-forge geoplot Or install from PyPi: pip install forecast-tools Remove environment (deactivate first): conda env remove -n temp_env Export environment to yml file (activate first). This exports all packages with version numbers (use actual greater sign, rather than [greater than] for export - YouTube description won't allow me to use it!): conda env export [greater than] environment.yml Set up environment from yml file: conda env create -f environment.yml An example simple yml file (we can put version numbers on some or all packages if we like with =, or with == for pip packages, but without version numbers Anaconda will work out best versions to use, though this may take some time): name: scipy_env channels: - defaults - conda-forge dependencies: - jupyterlab - matplotlib - numpy - pip - pandas - scikit-learn - scipy - spyder - pip: - simpy

title: Paper: using Deep Reinforcement Learning agents to solve the Ambulance Location Problem
details: Paper: GitHub: Developing an OpenAI Gym-compatible framework and simulation environment for testing Deep Reinforcement Learning agents solving the Ambulance Location Problem. The simulation environment, using SimPy and OpenAI gym, provides an environment where: * Incidents occurs in areas within a world with fixed dimensions. The geographic pattern of incidents may change throughout the day. * When an incident occurs, ambulances are dispatched from fixed dispatch points; the closest free ambulance is used. * The ambulance collects a patient and conveys them to the closest hospital. * The ambulance is then allocated, by an agent, to any dispatch point. The ambulance travels to that dispatch point where it becomes available to respond to incidents (the ambulance may also be allocated while travelling to a dispatch point, depending on simulation environment settings). * The job of the agent is to allocate ambulances to dispatch points in order to minimise the time from incident to arrival of ambulance at the scene of the incident. The paper (with code repository) implements a range of Deep Q Network architectures to solve this problem. Long tutorial (with code) on Q learning applied to controlling the number of staffed beds in a simple hospital simulation: The learning hospital - a basic Deep RL system. title: Transforming urgent and emergency care with real-time intelligence in Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin
details: Faced with growing pressure on urgent and emergency care (UEC) services, Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin Integrated Care Board (STW ICB) developed an innovative UEC Dashboard to deliver near real-time insight across the whole system—from NHS 111 and ambulance services to emergency departments, hospital flow, and community-based care. What sets this dashboard apart is its integration of NHS England’s Making Data Count methodology, with advanced Statistical Process Control (SPC) charts at its core. These enable frontline teams and system leaders to detect variation, identify trends, and respond quickly to emerging pressures. The solution is underpinned by an automated SSIS-driven data pipeline and a robust SQL-based data warehouse. Using a star-schema model, data flows securely into Power BI through an On-Premises Gateway for regular, reliable refreshes. Users can interrogate data at multiple time intervals—daily to yearly—tailored to operational needs. The results have been transformative: faster, smarter decisions; a shared language for performance; and a system-wide shift toward data-driven action. Recognised by NHS England’s Making Data Count national and regional teams as a benchmark model, the dashboard has directly contributed to improved system performance and played a pivotal role in supporting the ICB’s exit from legal oversight. This project exemplifies how strategic use of data and technology can enhance resilience, promote collaboration, and ultimately improve patient outcomes—demonstrating the power of workplace technology to drive system-wide improvement in the most high-pressure environments. Craig Lovatt, Senior Business Intelligence Lead (NHS Shropshire, Telford and Wreking) Kirsty Dyass, Quality Analyst (NHS Shropshire, Telfird and Wrekin) Craig Kynaston, Head of Business Intelligence and Analytics (Shropshire Telford and Wrekin ICB)

title: Building and implementing a patient non- attendance prediction system using commonly available data
details: "Introduction Missed diagnostic endoscopy appointments (“did not attend”, or DNA) negatively affect cancer outcomes by delaying treatment and worsening prognosis. DNAs also waste clinical resources and lengthen waiting times. Based on historical DNA data, we developed a machine learning–based predictive model, allowing for targeted interventions for patients at greater risk of non-attendance. Aim, Methods, Results Aim: To use PAS (Patient Administrative System) data to identify patients most at risk of not attending their upcoming endoscopy. High-risk patients are then contacted by a Health Navigator, who can offer targeted support and improve attendance rates. Methods: We trained an XGBoost model on 39,447 endoscopy appointments across six hospitals over the course of two years. The model predicted binary outcomes (DNA vs. attendance), optimised for AUROC and calibration error. Key predictors included prior DNAs, socio-economic deprivation (IMD), rurality, age, gender, and procedure type. Results: Patients with ≥10% predicted DNA risk were called by healthcare navigators over a 12 week period. Compared with a 17% baseline DNA rate, calling high risk patients reduced DNAs to 5% among contacted patients and 11% overall. Across 650 monitored appointments, 52 DNAs were recorded; scaling suggests ~150 annual DNAs could be prevented. Hence, the calls achieved a ~10% reduction in DNA rates. Impact (50 words) The project has led to an estimated saving of £37k per year. It also shaped system-level approaches to tackling health inequalities, informing our Trust’s Lifelong Care Strategy and influenced local policy (including prison pathways). Expansion of this approach is underway across five additional services, including a collaboration with Local Authorities. Integration into the booking software Healthcall is planned, embedding predictive analytics into routine practice to improve access and equity. Lessons learned Predicting patients’ DNA risk is possible using basic data taken from Patient Administrative Systems. These predictions can be used to perform an intervention with tangible benefits for both patients and hospitals. There are diverse reasons for which patients don’t attend their appointments, both personal and systemic, with different strategies to tackle them. Richard Bilsborough, Data Scientist/Information Specialist (Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust) Fabian Beigang, Data Scientist / Information Specialist (Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust) Chris Wilcockson, Public Health Analyst (Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust)

title: Semi-automated REDCap-R reporting workflow to support scotland's MAT standards
details: "Monitoring Scotland’s Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) Standards is essential for the National mission on ensuring timely and consistent access to care for people affected by substance use. In order to reduce barriers for frontline staff, we developed a semi-automated reporting approach that combines REDCap, a secure data-collection platform, with R flexdashboard and Posit Connect. In this talk, we show an example of how the reports and processes were implemented with usability a main priority. The semi-automated design reduces manual handling versus spreadsheet workflows, strengthens information governance, and increases data availability without claiming full automation. The approach is scalable to additional MAT Standards and adaptable to other NHS reporting domains where timely, secure insights are required. Analysts refresh an R workflow to generate dashboards that summarise the data in clear graphical formats—such as scatter plots and other visualisations—before securely distributing them to Alcohol and Drug Partnerships (ADPs). By focusing on plots rather than descriptive statistics (e.g., means and medians), the dashboards make it easier for both analysts and non-analysts to quickly identify key information, enabling ADPs to spot gaps and track improvement more effectively. This work demonstrates how combining established digital tools (REDCap, R, Posit Connect) with analyst-led refresh can create a sustainable, governance-compliant reporting infrastructure that helps frontline teams act on data, not just collect it" Manqiu Xiong, Information Analyst (NHS Lothian)

title: Evaluating the impact of Right Care, Right Person
details: "Right Care, Right Person (RCRP) is being implemented across police forces in England and Wales with the aim of ensuring that vulnerable people get the right support from the right agency. RCRP ensures calls for service relating to mental health are dealt with by the right service, and the police are working in partnership with other agencies to achieve this. Suffolk Constabulary implemented RCRP from October 2023, starting with calls for service relating to concern for welfare and later including those relating to walk outs from healthcare facilitates and AWOL from mental health establishments, transportation of patients and section 136 Mental Health Act/voluntary mental health patients. Suffolk Police and the Suffolk & North-East Essex Integrated Care Board commissioned the Suffolk Office of Data & Analytics (SODA) to evaluate the wider implications of RCRP to ensure that members of the public are indeed receiving the ‘right care’. Since the launch of RCRP, SODA has collated quarterly data from relevant partners. The data is visualised through a Power BI dashboard, which details how Welfare and Mental Health incidents are dealt with by the police and, if referred under RCRP, where referrals are made. This data is then linked to trends in ambulance call outs, A&E visits and NHS 111 calls, as well as local Specialist Mental Health Services and Suffolk County Council's Children's and Adults Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hubs. Although there were concerns about the impact that RCRP might have on services, we have found that the impact has not been as great as initially feared. We intend to continue to monitor trends to see if this changes. In November 2025, SODA is scheduled to follow up changes in call/attendance volumes with qualitative research to understand whether these are due to RCRP or if other factors could be behind these changes. Stephen Parsons, Advanced Analyst C Researcher(Suffolk Office of Data C Analytics)

title: Site-level Covid-19 vaccine demand forecasting: Efficiency across NHS vaccination sites
details: Seasonal COVID-19 vaccination campaigns in England require distributing millions of doses to almost 7,000 sites. The Targeted Deployment Model (TDM) currently manages deployment, balancing site stock levels against expected demand. However, the existing forecasting approach is deterministic and can be inaccurate, leading to over- or under supply, stock wastage, and inefficiencies. Improving forecast accuracy is essential to optimise resource use and support timely delivery. Aim To develop a more accurate site-level demand forecasting model, so that automated orders generated by TDM better reflect true local demand. Methods We used historical data on vaccination events, bookings, and site characteristics to train and evaluate a multivariate gradient boosting model (LightGBM). Feature engineering was critical to adapt this tree-based method for time series forecasting. Forecasts were produced at site level with a 14-day horizon and evaluated using walk-forward validation to replicate real-world conditions. Models were benchmarked against the existing TDM forecast using MAE, SMAPE, and bias. To capture variation, sites were clustered by demand patterns (e.g. advance bookings vs walk-ins) and activity size, and accuracy assessed across these groups. The forecasting pipeline was designed for scalability to nearly 7,000 sites and for integration into TDM, ensuring outputs could be used directly in deployment decisions. Results LightGBM provided the best balance of speed, accuracy, and flexibility, delivering an approximate 20% improvement in accuracy compared to the deterministic base model. That is, forecast performance across sites yielded a mean absolute error of 4.88 vaccinations and a symmetric mean absolute percentage error of 65.6%, with Bias around 25%. Clustering sites by demand behaviour improved interpretability and highlighted where forecasts diverged most from current allocations (e.g. walk-in heavy versus advance-booking sites). Daily retraining was successfully implemented to ensure forecasts remained relevant throughout campaigns. Impact This work informed NHS England’s planning for the October 2025 campaign. Improved forecasts were integrated into the TDM pipeline to automate stock orders, and better match supply with demand across thousands of sites. Liliana Valles, Senior Data Science Manager (NHS England) Scarlett Kynoch, Data Scientist (NHS England) Ilyas Ag Sidiyene, (NHS England)

title: Virtual fracture clinic improves boast compliance, patient outcomes, and delivers cost savings in lower socio-economic areas
details: Background: Lower socio-economic regions have higher pressures on emergency services. Virtual services can reduce the demand on secondary care. We aim to assess the effect of virtual fracture clinics (VFC) on compliance with BOAST guidelines, patient reported outcomes and hospital metrics in an inner city setting with higher levels of social deprivation. Methods: A closed-loop prospective audit was performed, comparing outcomes from January to December 2024 (pre-VFC) to February to March 2025 (post-VFC). BOAST 72-hour breach rates, discharge rates, did-not-attend (DNA) rates, surgical conversion rates, patient satisfaction, and projected cost savings were assessed. Results: New attendances reduced from 45 to 27 per day. On average, 18 patients were assessed each day in VFC, with a discharge rate of 32.3%, saving 155 appointments. Required face-to-face (F2F) fracture clinic slots were reduced by 40.9%, from 110 pre-VFC to 65 post-VFC. F2F DNA rates reduced from 23.5% (n=863) pre-VFC to 8.3% (n=26) post-VFC, with a 1.2% (n=9) DNA rate for VFC calls. Pre-VFC, 9.8% of surgical and emergency cases were incorrectly triaged to fracture clinic; this reduced to 1.2% post-VFC. 72-hour BOAST fracture clinic guideline breaches decreased from 37.4% (n=2449) to 14.5% (n=70). 84% of patients preferred VFC over waiting in clinic, where wait times were over 90 minutes. Projected annual cost savings from reduced attendances exceeded £100,000. Conclusion: VFC markedly improved BOAST compliance, reduced non-urgent fracture clinic attendances and DNA rates. It expedited urgent cases to on-call pathways. There were exceptional operational cost savings. VFC led to consultant-level decision-making at an earlier point of care, preventing harm and redistributing departmental resources to patient benefit. This audit demonstrated VFC to be a successful model despite high levels of deprivation and one of the largest cohorts of non-English-speaking patients in the UK. Rania Khan, Foundation Year 2 Doctor (NHS England)

title: Modelling renal care from progression to diagnosis
details: We don’t have sufficient capacity to meet future needs for renal services. The Strategy Unit, working collaboratively with Midlands Renal Network, have built a hybrid simulation model of renal care from the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) to kidney replacement therapy (KRT). This collection of models projects both demand, the number of patients flowing into KRT for the next 10 years, and capacity, where they’ll be in the system (dialysis type/living with transplant). Additionally, the simulation allows for the evaluation of interventions for patients at all stages of renal care from the impact of new drugs and prevention strategies to direct changes to KRT care pathways. This work is crucial for informing and evidencing future renal plans. Our aim is to role this out nationally over the coming year and open-source our model to improve access and model sustainability. Lucy Morgan, Analytics Manager (Simulation) (Strategy Unit) Sally Thompson, Senior Healthcare Analyst (Strategy Unit)
