title: The GP resilience matrix: A strategic tool for targeted primary care support
details: Primary care resilience is often only recognised at the point of crisis. We set out to make earlier signals visible — so that practices under pressure can be supported sooner, protecting patient access and staff sustainability. The GP Resilience Matrix was first developed in Excel and became a widely used, trusted product. It integrated 40+ indicators across clinical quality (QOF), workforce (FTE per 10k), demand/flow (GPAD; 111/999/UTC/ED per 10k), patient experience (GPPS), and context (IMD, CQC). Standardisation with z-scores enabled fair comparison, and practices were banded from “Higher Achieving” to “Review Identified”. While effective, Excel became labour-intensive to maintain and too rigid for live use, creating inefficiencies that affected timeliness. We rebuilt in Power BI; retaining the analytics while improving usability and sustainability. This directly responds to the HACA 2025 theme by showing how analysis can rise to the challenge of shaping future-ready systems. Data was structured into a relational model; DAX calculated scores, composites and bands. We used the project to stress-test our “woodyard” BI operating model — data investigation, engineering, development, visualisation — managed through weekly updates and mapping sessions. Key user changes included: maps for geographic context, flexible filters, deeper drill-through, curated table exports, and adjustable criteria so thresholds/weights can reflect local priorities. These reduced dependence on analysts and made the tool practical in live PCN and ICB meetings. Demo feedback was strong: users noted it offered more flexibility and insight than national platforms. Locally, colleagues have already used it in DES/S96 support conversations to benchmark and prompt improvement, helping target support upstream in primary care and ensure resources are allocated more equitably. By reducing manual effort and streamlining refresh, the rebuild also improved system flow and reduced wasted effort, freeing analyst time for higher-value work. Analytics only helps if people can work with it; rigour must balance with UX; our schema build could have been more efficient; diverse team perspectives added value; resourcing and stakeholder availability constrained pace. Moving from Excel to Power BI reduced maintenance burden, improving timeliness and sustainability. Next steps: publish a documentation package (business rules/user guidance), automate refresh, and validate whether resilience bands predict future stress. This evolution shows how analysis can move from a static product to a dynamic, explainable model at the heart of resilience planning for future health systems. Ritesh Raj, Population Health C Strategy Lead Analyst (NHS Kent and Medway ICB)"

title: Making easy the default: Driving digital uptake in NHS 111 dental and prescription pathways using Behaviour Change Theory
details: High call volumes to NHS 111, often from low acuity callers, are straining urgent and emergency care services. Using the EAST (easy, attractive, social, timely) framework, new messaging was developed and trialled to encourage London patients to use digital services for dental and prescription needs. The aim was to measurably increase the uptake of digital services, achieving a channel shift for patients from traditional phone-based services to digital pathways. A randomised controlled trial (RCT) was conducted to assess the effect of three messaging formats on digital service uptake. Three formats of message content (Easy, Social, Control) were informed by post‑call patient experience survey responses from over 12,000 patients and structured using the EAST behaviour change framework. Patients contacting NHS 111 for dental or prescription queries were randomly assigned to receive each message type. Trends in uptake and the relative performance of each message formats were evaluated using Statistical Process Control (SPC) methods. A significant, sustained increase in digital uptake was identified, with ‘Easy’ messaging outperforming others. Uptake improved by 7–12% (dental), 8–12% (repeat prescriptions), and 5–8% (emergency medication) versus control, without adverse impact on 24‑hour call‑back rates. Adoption of the approach is now underway. Estimated uptake suggests more than 18,000 London patients seeking dental or prescription services annually will shift to digital services, equivalent to 285 eight‑hour call handler workdays saved. Analysis identified many connected factors influencing results that SPC or RCT alone couldn’t fully demonstrate. System dynamics can map these links, test changes, and find tipping points that inform more adaptable decisions alongside regular monitoring. Efejiro Ashano, Senior Data Analyst (Guys and St. Thomas NHS) Kate Lambe, (Health Innovation Network South London) Helen Sheldon, (Health Innovation Network South London)"

title: Direct and indirect impacts of industrial action on emergency department attendances in England, 2022-2024: A causal mediation analysis with 20 hospitals
details: "Background Between December 2022 and July 2024, the English National Health Service saw 27 periods of industrial action over 78 days, involving hospital and ambulance staff. We examine the impacts of industrial action on the Emergency Department (ED). Methods This observation study of unplanned attendances at 20 major (Type 1) EDs in England from August 2022 to July 2024, selected sites with high-quality data across emergency, inpatient, and imaging records. Our primary outcome was the patient’s duration in the ED along with indicators of a strike by one or more of the following staff groups at the mid-point of the patient’s ED stay: (1) resident/junior doctors, (2) consultants, (3) both residents and consultants, (4) paramedics, and (5) nurses. Effects were estimated with accelerated failure time, linear and generalised linear regression models with fixed and random effects (hospital level) within a causal mediation analysis. Results The average duration of ED attendances reduced on days affected by residents’ strikes [-12.6%, 95% CI -10.4% to -14.8%], consultant strikes [-5.6%, -2.7% to -8.4%], paramedic strikes [-4.5%, -2.0% to -6.8%], but increased when both residents and consultants were on strike simultaneously [+7.2%, +3.8% to +10.7%]. There were no significant changes to ED durations during nurse strikes [-1.7%, -1.5% to 4.7%]. Changes in emergency inpatient occupancy explained a proportion of the change in average ED durations (resident doctor 10.4%, consultants 53.3%, combined doctors 5.4%, and paramedics 14.3%). The impact of strikes on ED attendance volumes was mixed. The net effect of these changes explained 1.5%, 16.8% and 28.8% of the change in average ED durations observed during residents, combined doctor, and paramedic strikes respectively. During the residents’ strikes, patients were more likely to receive treatments in ED [adjusted incident risk ratio 1.013, 1.008 to 1.018], but less likely to be admitted [adjusted odds ratio 0.963, 0.946 to 0.980]. Efforts to meet the 4-hour target intensified during the resident, consultant and combined doctors strike, but reduced during the nurse and paramedic strikes. This explained 2.7%, and 17.1% of the changes in average ED durations observed during the resident and consultant strikes respectively. There were substantial reductions in many forms of planned hospital care during the resident, consultant and combined doctor strikes, but these did not lead to statistically significant changes in ED durations. Conclusion The findings suggest that industrial action—particularly during resident doctor and consultant strikes—was associated with reduced ED durations, due in part, to increased emergency bed availability, reduced ED demand, more intensive patient management, and heightened focus on meeting performance targets. However, most reductions during resident doctor strikes could not be fully explained by measurable factors, indicating other unobserved changes in hospital resources, operations or behaviours. Notably, while reductions in planned care activities were substantial, they did not significantly impact ED flow. Steven Wyatt, Head of Research C Policy (Strategy Unit)"

title: Turning insight into action: Using data to improve asthma outcomes in Dorset
details: "Introduction Many people live with asthma as a long-term condition. Up to 2020, data showed that Dorset had higher asthma mortality rates than other areas in the South West. Overuse of Short-Acting Beta Agonists (SABA) is linked to poor outcomes and increased risk of death. Dorset needed a way to better understand and address prescribing patterns contributing to these risks. Aim, Methods and Results The aim was to use data to identify patterns of SABA overprescribing and support practices in improving asthma care by increasing the use of preventative treatments. Dorset Intelligence and Insight Service (DiiS) developed reports highlighting excessive SABA prescribing across Primary Care Networks (PCNs). These insights enabled practices to review prescribing behaviours and identify patients at risk. Some PCNs used this data to audit care plans and promote the use of inhaled corticosteroids, aligning with national asthma management guidelines. The granularity of DiiS data, updated daily and available at person level, allowed targeted interventions. Practices could focus on individuals with high SABA use and adjust treatment plans. This proactive approach supported better clinical decision-making and population health management. Across Dorset, SABA overuse declined more rapidly than in other Integrated Care Systems (ICSs) in the South West. PCNs that reduced SABA prescribing saw corresponding drops in asthma-related hospital admissions. Mortality rates from asthma also decreased, suggesting improved outcomes linked to data-informed care. Impact The project influenced prescribing practices and clinical decision-making across Dorset. DiiS insights enabled timely, targeted action, supporting safer asthma management and contributing to reduced admissions and mortality. Lessons Learned Real-time, granular data is essential for identifying variation, understanding its causes, and driving effective interventions. DiiS enabled clinicians to act quickly, improving care quality and outcomes. This work shows how data and technology can help reduce risk, personalise care, and support strategic priorities in population health. " Paul Wilding, Dorset Healthcare University NHS Foundation Trust William McConnell, Dorset County Hospital NHS Foundation Trust

title: Predicting the demand for care homes with service user journeys
details: "Adult Social Care (ASC) provides support to those who find it difficult to perform day-to-day tasks. ASC provides support based on the need of the resident. Those that live in care homes typically receive a higher level of support, at higher cost, than those that live in the community. Residents can move between care types based on their needs. Understanding these transitions will inform resource planning and help design interventions to maximise the time that people can live in their own homes. The aim of the project is to model user transitions between different ASC packages. We want to know what characteristics influence service users' transitions by looking at the long-term journey of an individual and how likely they are to go from one type of care to another. We applied a multi-state model to data from adults receiving a local authority social care package between 2020 and 2024. We estimated the probability of transitions across three states: Community-based, Care home, and End-of-life. This approach allowed us to quantify user journeys over time and identify factors related to transitions. From the transition probability matrix at 1 year, people receiving community-based care had a 3% probability of moving into a Care home. This increased to 12% at year 5. Differences by gender were seen, with men in a Care home having a 30% probability of moving into Community based care versus 13% for women at year 5. The Model will forecast the number of care home places that will be needed over the next 10 years. Findings are being discussed with stakeholders to consider what targeted initiatives could be tested to lower the probability of transition into a care home. The model could be extended by adding another state for people not receiving ASC." Mai Stafford (Brent Council) Adshayan Saravanamuthu, (Brent Council)

title: Evolving a national diabetes learning health system: Lessons from trials embedded within a national audit
details: Introduction: Some patients do not receive recommended care. For example, there are big differences in how well primary care networks help patients to reduce blood glucose levels and associated risks. To improve care, national organisations provide interventions (e.g. webinars) to clinical teams. It is not known how best to target interventions (e.g. to address higher risks faced by young adults with type 2 diabetes) or whether such interventions lead to improvement or are value-for-money. Aim & methods: Through collaboration, we have embedded a cluster randomised controlled trial within the National Diabetes Audit to evaluate interventions it delivers to improve the care and outcomes for people with diabetes. Design: Efficient 3-arm cluster randomised trial with process and economic evaluations using routine NDA data. Participants: All 1283 Primary Care Networks in England Interventions: Medium-intensity feedback facilitation, delivered through webinars and multi-site calls; Low-intensity feedback facilitation contains similar content delivered through e-learning and email. Comparator: Usual care (waitlist control group) Outcomes: Blood glucose of young adults (18-39years) with type 2 diabetes and baseline above NICE-recommended levels. Theory-informed exploration of intervention implementation, engagement fidelity and tailoring. Investigation of cost-effectiveness and budget impact. Results & Impact: This is our second embedded evaluation. Each pragmatic trial gives rigorous information about (cost-)effectiveness to the funders and providers of routinely delivered interventions. Such information enables the national audit to continually improve care and outcomes, and in doing so become a learning health system. Lessons learned: We endorse calls to move beyond designing and delivering one-off trials and towards sustainable learning health systems that bring together routine data, evaluation capabilities and intervention providers. Such learning health systems can efficiently trial multiple improvement interventions to target inequalities and implementation challenges. We will open a discussion about factors that enable or hinder embedding rigorous evaluations of implementation strategies within healthcare systems. Michael Sykes, Vice-Chancellor's Fellow C National Audit Improvement Lead (Northumbria University National Diabetes Audit) Dr Bethan Copsey, Principal Moedical Statistician (University of Leeds)

title: The Woodyard Model: Reducing waste and delivering impact
details: Introduction BI teams often face the challenge of being data rich but insight poor. Requests arrive from different directions, similar work starts in parallel, and duplication wastes valuable time. We are developing a “Woodyard” operating model — a structured flow from data investigation → engineering → development → visualisation — to cut waste and strengthen the quality of BI outputs. Sponsored by our Chief Data & Analytics Officer, the Woodyard gives analysts, engineers, and DV specialists a common framework. It is still a work in progress but already showing value. Methods and Results We applied the Woodyard to projects such as the GP Resilience Matrix and a consolidation exercise where overlapping requests were identified as sharing a common dataset. Instead of multiple builds, engineering effort was focused once and re-used. Weekly updates, requirements mapping, and a shared backlog encouraged collaboration across teams. DV standards — consistent maps, filters, drill paths, and curated tables — made outputs reproducible, reusable, and easier to use in live meetings. Impact Products developed through the Woodyard have been more sustainable and practical. The GP Resilience Matrix, for example, is now used in DES/S96 support conversations to benchmark practices and target resources equitably. Consolidation reduced duplication and freed analyst and engineering time for higher-value work. By getting usable DV into meetings faster, the Woodyard has helped decision-makers act sooner to support services and patients. We believe this approach could become a cost-saving BI model that is reproducible across ICBs, cutting duplication nationally and supporting collaboration in the current pressured NHS environment. Lessons Learned Reuse must be visible at intake, next time we would build these checks earlier to prevent duplication before work begins. Standards and cadence reduce drift, and sponsorship helps embed them, but resource alignment with engineering and limited stakeholder time remain constraints. We also learned that communication across teams is critical: where requests are shared and challenged, duplication falls. The Woodyard is still evolving, but even partial adoption has improved flow, reduced waste, and strengthened collaboration. Shevon Licorish, Head of Data Visualisation (NHS Kent and Medway ICB)"
