title: NHS Theatre Tariffs for lower limb surgery: An unbalanced system?
details: Within the NHS, nationally set tariffs are based on average procedure costs and often fail to reflect resources needed for complex patients, disadvantaging main sites. Elective hubs focus on high-volume, low-risk cases, leaving main hospitals to deliver complex care at a loss. Unpredictable case complexity also reduces theatre throughput, limiting the spread of fixed costs. This study examined whether national tariff income covers costs of elective lower limb procedures, identified key drivers of financial overruns, and evaluated the impact of list efficiency on financial outcomes. A retrospective financial analysis was performed on 44 elective lower limb procedures across 13 theatre lists (12/09/24–29/10/24). Finance data enabled calculation of profitability at list and procedure level. Example lists were modelled to test the impact of additional cases and efficiency changes on net profitability. The service incurred a net loss of £99,477, with costs (£366,433) exceeding tariff income (£266,956). Theatre time was the largest cost driver (up to 52%). Hip procedures had higher ward (19.4% vs 9.7%) and implant costs (10.5% vs 5.8%) than knees, while foot & ankle procedures had minimal implant costs (1.2%). Modelling showed increasing volume, such as adding arthroscopies, improved efficiency, spread fixed costs, and could make lists profitable without staffing, highlighting throughput as a key determinant of financial performance. This evidence has shifted internal strategy towards increasing procedural volume and strengthened advocacy for enhanced recovery pathways. Externally, it supports national tariff reform, advocating fairer reimbursement of complex cases, highlighting risks of service fragmentation, and emphasising the need for tariffs reflecting patient complexity and local costs. Efficiency gains alone cannot offset a tariff system misaligned with complex care. Future work should include patient complexity scores in financial models and audit elective hubs to demonstrate risk transfer. Sustainability requires internal optimisation and advocacy for tariff reform reflecting true cost drivers. Canan Metin, Senior House Officer (Royal Free Hospital NHS Foundation Trust) Satish Janipreddy, (Royal Free Hospital NHS Foundation Trust) Sanjay Sinha, (Royal Free Hospital NHS Foundation Trust)"
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Actionable insights to reduce delayed discharge in day surgery wards: The power of linked data and clinical-analytical collaborations
details: In day surgery units, patients not discharged on the day of their procedure (delayed discharges, DD) strain local healthcare resources and impact outcomes. The national target for day surgery discharge is that 91% of cases are same-day discharges (SDD) but only 85% SDD is achieved. The Day Surgery Unit (DSU) in the RIE hospital (NHS Lothian, Scotland) aspires to an ambitious target of 95% SDD but has a 68% achievement rate. They requested analytical support to understand what factors predict delayed discharges and how strongly each factor affected delayed discharges in order to develop evidence-based interventions and operational improvements to increase SDD. We linked multiple data sources to create a custom-built database for the RIE-DSU using a shareable RAP in R. We used generalised linear mixed models to identify which demographic, service-related (operational), medical practice factors (total opioids, specific opioids, antiemetics, anaesthetic group, procedure), and patient health factors, including post-operative outcomes (pain score and nausea), affected DD and estimated their effect size. We found that most significant factors were related to service operations and medical practices and thus can be changed or planned for. We collaborated with clinicians and hospital managers to translate estimates into four evidence-based actionable insights to optimise SDD. This work resulted in implementing evidence-based changes in operational metrics, post-operative pain and nausea management, and prescribing practices of opioids and antiemetics to improve DSU efficiency and reduce DD. This project demonstrates the power of analysing linked data (theatres, inpatients, outpatients, GP, community and hospital prescribing) to achieve strategic objectives in a reproducible way. Nora Villamil Buenrostro, Senior Information Analyst/Statistician (NHS Scotland)"
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Delay-related harm: Direct and indirect impacts of boarding medical patients in the emergency department on the urgent and emergency care pathway
details: Accident and Emergency (A&E) crowding and long waits are a widespread issue in our National Health Service. We analysed three years of data from three A&E departments, using regression to quantify how medical patient boarding—a major contributor to delays—correlated with inpatient length of stay, mortality and readmission rate, ambulance delays, and A&E wait times. Our findings reveal that increased medical boarding is associated with longer ambulance response and handover times, as well as extended inpatient stays and higher risk of adverse outcomes for admitted medical patients. This study demonstrates how medical patient boarding generates a ripple effect, impacting not only the boarded patients but also ambulance services and other A&E users. We’ll also discuss how these results have been translated into a deployed dashboard, providing real-time insights to operational managers in the NHS. This tool allows for dynamic monitoring of boarding impacts, enabling data-driven interventions to improve A&E efficiency and patient flow, ultimately impacting broader healthcare delivery. The data highlights the interconnectedness of A&E processes and the potential for actionable insights. Nick Howlett, Senior Data Scientist (NHS Bristol, North Somerset and South Gloucestershire ICB)"
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Developing a short-term demand and capacity planning model for gastrointestinal endoscopy services using ordinary differential equations
details: Background: Gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy services face challenges in mounting demand and constrained budgets, particularly post-pandemic. Demand and capacity modelling has become essential for optimising resources across various services in the NHS. Objective: To develop a compartmental Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) model for short-term demand and capacity planning in a local endoscopy unit. Methods: Historical operational data over 4 years was obtained from the Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust and utilised for modelling. The model was constructed incorporating different compartments that represent various stages within the service pathway stratified by procedure types, including referrals, waitlists, admissions, in-procedures, and discharges. A set of scenario tests was conducted to examine varying operational strategies, including switching the referral pathway (i.e., transferring 50% of referrals between urgent and routine pathways), temporary capacity loss, capacity allocation adjustment (i.e., modifying the capacity allocation ratios between upper and lower GI procedures), etc. Results: The model successfully outputs crucial operational metrics on a weekly basis, demonstrating satisfactory accuracy. Scenario testing illustrated the model’s ability to provide quantitative insights into the impacts of changing the referral dynamics and capacity allocation settings. For instance, we found that reducing the carrying capacity for either oesophagogastroduodenoscopy or colonoscopy resulted in an increase in both active and planned corresponding waiting lists, while this effect was notably more prominent for colonoscopy. Conclusion: The model offers a powerful tool for endoscopy service planning, enabling managers to anticipate fluctuations in demand and experiment with various strategies. Shuhe Li, Graduate Research Assistant (University of Exeter)"
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Understanding NHS waiting lists: Insights from the Networked Data Lab in North West London
details: Elective care waiting lists in England have reached unprecedented levels, with over 7.6 million patients waiting and only 59.1% treated within the NHS’s 18-week target. This study, conducted by the Networked Data Lab in North West London (NWL), provides a comprehensive analysis of waiting list dynamics, focusing on hip replacements and cardiothoracic surgery—two specialties of local and national significance. Using the Discover dataset, one of Europe’s largest depersonalised linked health records, we examined over 2.5 million patient pathways. Our descriptive analysis revealed disparities in wait times across age, gender, deprivation, and frailty. Notably, younger and more deprived patients experienced longer waits, while those with severe frailty were prioritised. However, these patterns varied by specialty, underscoring the risk of ecological fallacy in global-level interpretations. Our causal analysis employed a difference-in-difference design to isolate the impact of prolonged waiting on healthcare utilisation and costs. For hip replacements, patients waiting longer than 18 weeks had a statistically significant increase of 1.10 GP appointments (p=0.001) and 0.09 emergency admissions (p=0.018) per person during the post-operative period compared to those treated within target timeframes, suggesting a potential long-term cost burden. Cardiothoracic findings were inconclusive due to small sample sizes. Public involvement was central to our approach. A Patient and Carer Advisory Group shaped the research questions, validated interim findings, and highlighted the emotional and financial toll of waiting. Their insights revealed gaps in support and communication, reinforcing the need for policies that promote “waiting well. Findings have been shared with the NWL Acute Care Board and will inform ongoing engagement exercises on planned care. Future iterations will refine the causal design, expand follow-up periods, and explore missing data patterns to better capture long-term impacts. We recommend further research into private care substitution and disparities in clock stop recording to ensure more inclusive, representative analysis. Marcus Yarwood, Senior Quantitative Insights Manager (Imperial College Health Partners) Alex Cheuk, Data Scientist (Imperial College Health Partners) Melanie Leis, Director of Policy and Analysis (Imperial College London)"
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Evaluation planning and implementation: Adapting analytical approaches for complex health problems and interventions.
details: • Introduction: Health problem presentations are becoming increasingly complex. There is a need for new approaches that show the value of health improvement initiatives. Reflection from the health and care workforce, about existing evaluation guidance, includes that ‘there seems too much, yet too little out there’ and how ‘to start doing’ an evaluation. • Describe the aim, methods or approaches, and results: We aimed to develop an evaluation training guide to enhance analytical literacy amongst non-analytical professionals, and to embed evaluation planning into strategic commissioning approaches across an integrated care system. Participatory methods involved individual and group discussions, with a range of skills/expertise, including external partners and co-production lead. As a result, the evaluation guide was iteratively developed, comprising of a three-staged framework (scoping, co-designing the project’s change theory-logic model, and data analytics). In addition to clear steps for each stage, the guide introduces co-production and systems thinking as a holistic approach for complex problem-solving. Results show increased engagement in effective evaluation planning and implementation, contributing to high quality decision-making in health priorities (e.g. reducing health inequalities and supporting sexual violence survivors using the systems lens). • Impact: The published evaluation guide (with supporting webinars) is being used across commissioning organisations, to embed evaluation into projects from the onset. There is an increased awareness of and ability to implement evaluation methodologies, allowing basic processes to close the loop on strategic commissioning frameworks. The guide serves as a blueprint for evaluation across health and care organisations. • Lessons learned: Humans lie behind data. This is one of our guiding principles and reinforces the need to show the patient journey or process mapping, in addition to quantitative evaluation. " Lamiya Samad, Senior Evaluation Analyst (Suffolk and North East Essex ICS) Alexander Royan, Lead for Strategy and Healthcare Intelligence (NHS Suffolk and North East Essex Integrated Care Board)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Data-driven winter support for older people across an ICS
details: Introduction Problem: Cold weather disproportionately harms older people, driving primary care demand, admissions and excess mortality. Following changes to winter fuel eligibility, Dorset faced a larger cohort of financially vulnerable pensioners at risk of cold-related harm. Aim, Methods/Approach: We aimed to 1identify who and where to target support; 2 coordinate rapid, community-first interventions; 3 reduce avoidable system pressure while improving resident experience. The Dorset Intelligence & Insight Service DiiS) linked Mosaic profiling with pseudonymised GP registers to flag residents aged ≥66 with respiratory/cardiovascular conditions. We produced ward-level hot-spots and actionable outreach lists, then convened fortnightly 30-minute stand-ups NHS, councils, VCSE, housing, police, utilities. Using an agile loop, partners tested micro-interventions—targeted comms, PCN-led Winter Wellness events, “make every contact count” prompts for social prescribers/field staff, and a StayWell Financially hub warm spaces, benefits advice, fraud prevention, utilities support —and iterated using rapid feedback. Information governance followed existing DPIAs/DSAs; data were minimised and shared on a need-to-know basis. Results: -44,000 pensioners were estimated at risk; ~25,000 likely not receiving Pension Credit. Fifteen partners actively contributed; -750 residents attended Winter Wellness events in priority wards. Directionally, average primary care contacts fell within the at-risk cohort during the intervention period (acknowledging winter confounders). Front-line feedback cited earlier help-seeking and reduced duplication through shared collateral and joint outreach. Impact Decisions, Policy, Learning: Findings directly informed targeted communications, practice-level outreach and partner deployment in 20 hot-spot wards. The cadence, artefacts and governance have since been adopted for Ageing Well and carers’ support, influencing ICS planning for Winter 25/26. Lessons learned (What we’d do differently): Start with a smaller set of high-signal variables to accelerate onboarding; pre-agree a simple outcomes framework (event uptake, successful signposts, proxy service use) to reduce measurement lag; embed resident voice more systematically short structured prompts at point of contact); and stand up a lightweight shared collateral library earlier to cut duplication further. Rob Dabbs, Deputy Head of Analytics (Dorset Intelligence and Insight Service) Izzy Webb, Lead Business Intelligence Partner (Dorset Intelligence and Insight Service)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Emergency department attendances: Intersectionality, demography and patient complexity
details: "In this paper, we present systematic evidence on the composition and growth of patient demand for Emergency Department services at University Hospitals of Leicester from July 2022 to November 2024. We use a combination of descriptive analysis and least squares regression to document five key facts. First, adult attendances consistently outnumber paediatric attendances by a factor of 3 whilst seasonal and long-term growth in attendances is driven by paediatric activity. Second, the composition of actual ED attendances is not representative of UHL's overall population, with significant overrepresentation from ethnic minority groups and those from more deprived groups who, on average, visit ED with less acute representations. Third, there are no major changes to the composition of who visits ED, between 2022 and 2024, implying that growth is distributionally uniform with no clearly identifiable sub-group driving that growth over time. Fourth, white individuals and those from less deprived groups seem to wait longer. However, this is driven, almost entirely, by the fact that these white and less deprived attendees are older. It does not seem to be driven by more acute representations amongst these groups. Finally, over time, we find that demand for emergency department services is getting less concentrated amongst fewer sub-groups, when attendees are split by age-ethnicity-deprivation. This suggests that predicting demand for services by high-level demographic information will become more complex in the years to come" Ruw Abeyratne, Director of Health Equality and Inclusion (University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust) George Macdonald, Data Scientist (University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Quantifying categories of potentially mitigable hospital activity to support healthcare planning
details: "A key focus in current healthcare planning is on shifting care delivery from acute hospitals to community settings. This approach assumes that certain subsets of hospital activity can be mitigated with greater use of new or existing community services. To inform healthcare planning there is a need to understand the scale, trends, and regional variations in potentially mitigable hospital activity. We investigated 29 categories of potentially mitigable activity (CPMAs) that were developed as part of the New Hospital Programme Demand and Capacity model ( Using the Hospital Episode Statistics dataset we identified inpatient activity within these 29 categories, where there is potential for some activity to be moved to community services. We conducted descriptive analyses to show characteristics of activity within each CPMA and demonstrated the degree of overlap between the 29 categories. Comparisons of age and sex standardised rates of admissions and bed days show there is considerable variation in the scale of potentially mitigable activity between ICBs. Trends over time for England and by ICB, show that for some CPMAs, such as End-of-Life care, there has been a reduction in acute hospital activity. However, for other CPMAs, including older people with high frailty, chronic ambulatory sensitive conditions and acute alcohol related admissions, the standardised rates of hospital activity have been increasing in many regions. This analysis is helping ICBs, and others, to understand where there might be opportunities to reduce inpatient activity, in part through comparison to higher performing systems and could help inform decisions about shifting funding from acute services into primary and community care. The report and code are publicly available allowing others to replicate, interrogate and build upon the analyses " Sarah Lucas, Healthcare Analyst (Strategy Unit) Anya Ferguson, Healthcare Analyst (Strategy Unit)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: A model is for life, not just for Christmas: The power of multidisciplinary working in a business critical model rollout
details: "The Strategy Unit was engaged by the New Hospital Programme to develop a model that would predict future demand for acute care in the coming years to support in the sizing of new build hospitals. This talk tells a story in three parts: the preparatory stage of development of this model which involved slow thinking and careful planning, the ""baptism of fire"" of rolling the model out to multiple users and all the chaos and learning that came about from that, and the final phase of using all the experience from the early stages to build a model build by the NHS, for the NHS, fit for the future of demand modelling. Pivoting between these stages and changing our ways of working ""live"" as we delivered the model felt like building the track in front of the train as we sped along it and this talk will reflect not only the lessons learned from this process but also how we worked as a multidisciplinary analytic team to learn these lessons alongside the delivery. Finally the talk will explore next steps for our ways of working as the Unit continues to innovate in its delivery of complex projects using agile methods as well as the future of the model rollout. This builds on our vision of providing the NHS with the tools it needs to face its coming challenges- openly, transparently, for the whole health and care system." Karen Bradley, Principal Consultant (Strategy Unit) Chris Beeley, Head of Data Science (Strategy Unit)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Design a model for community pharmacy workforce with open source data
details: "This session demonstrates a forecasting model of the community pharmacy workforce supply and demand, not only for its own importance, but also for its broader implications in accommodating intervention scenarios and shifting demands from GPs to community pharmacies. The model uses an automated Python-based pipeline to ingest several datasets directly from publicly available sources, including the NHS Business Services Authority and ONS APIs. Additional open data publications, such as the Community Pharmacy Workforce Survey (CPWS) and GPhC registration data, are also used. Focusing on two key professions regulated by the General Pharmaceutical Council (GPhC)—pharmacists and pharmacy technicians—the model is built to inform workforce planning for NHS services delivered in high-street pharmacy premises. All code is managed on a GitHub repository, providing full transparency, version control, and a platform for team collaboration. The session will highlight how this reproducible and open framework can be used to improve the accuracy and efficiency of workforce planning for this vital part of the NHS, offering a practical tool for fellow analysts. The example model can be made freely available for widespread use, adaptation, and future model development of policy interventions. This work would have been tested with more scalable datasets, but was limited to data constraints that could have been considered for generating a synthetic dataset." Chaeyoon Kim, Data Scientist (NHS England)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Enhancing patient flow: Real-time prediction at a Swedish emergency department
details: "Problem: The Emergency Department (ED) at Sahlgrenska University Hospital faces daily challenges in securing beds for patients who require admission to hospital wards—a difficulty also encountered in the UK. Real-time predictions can offer actionable insights and foster a shared understanding of daily pressures by forecasting ED patient inflow by specialty, thus supporting better planning and coordination between the ED and hospital wards. Aim: The project aims to predict patient inflow from the ED at Sahlgrenska University Hospital by medical specialty, by testing the open-source prediction pipeline developed for this purpose at University College London Hospital (UCLH) on Sahlgrenska’s data. Method/process: The initial project phase focused on cleaning and preparing real-time data for the pipeline. Understanding the ED’s processes was key to accurate data interpretation. The second phase focused on replicating the procedure applied at UCLH by using the open-source Python package Patientflow and training predictive models. This allowed us to evaluate the models and directly compare their performance with those at UCLH. Technically, the results appear promising, and a pilot test will have taken place by the time of the conference talk. Results: We identified differences between the systems—such as ED targets in the original package not relevant at Sahlgrenska, which were adjusted accordingly. Despite more limited data at Sahlgrenska, technical performance was comparable in both settings. We plan to report on results following the pilot testing. Impact: One notable impact has been that the Sahlgrenska data science team has gained increased visibility among the ED clinicians. Additional impacts, particularly those related to the pilot testing, will be reported once the pilot study has been completed. Researcher Zella King, developer of Patientflow, and a Sahlgrenska data scientist who tested the pipeline at Sahlgrenska University Hospital will jointly present, highlighting the project's collaborative and cross-institutional nature. " Sara Lundell, Data Scientist (Sahlgrenska University Hospital) Zella King, Health Data Scientist (University College London)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Better Together: Supporting analysts and managers with RAP
details: "Many health and care analysts work alone, trying to implement reproducible analytical pipelines (RAP) without much local support. To help, The Strategy Unit has been running regular RAP drop-ins. These sessions provide a supportive space where both analysts and managers can share challenges, swap tips, and ask the “silly” questions without judgement. Common themes include navigating IT restrictions, upskilling teams with new tools, and handling data safely. The value of the drop-ins comes not from having all the answers, but from connecting people, sharing practical solutions, and learning together. This talk will highlight the questions we hear most often, the lessons learned so far, and how open, welcoming spaces help teams adopt RAP more effectively, supporting better decision-making and sustainable analytical practice across health and care systems." Rhian Davies, Senior Data Scientist (Strategy Unit) YiWen Hon, Data Scientist (Strategy Unit)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Modelling characteristics associated with the risk of a poor patient outcomes 90 days after discharge
details: "Aim To uncover which patient characteristics are driving poor outcomes (death, readmission and new long-term services) for patients in the 90 days following discharge, specifically assessing the impact of hospital discharge delays, given the known impact of deconditioning on patient health. Methods Linked Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Client Level Data (CLD) and ONS Deaths dataset in SQL. Then cleaned, derived new features and predicted outcomes using a logistic regression model on a sample of 1,000,000 patients discharged in 2024 in England. Results We found which variables were the most important features for predicting a poor outcome, and found an estimate for how much discharge delay contributes to poor outcomes (with everything else held constant). Impact Using this change in likelihood due to average length of delay, we were able to estimate the number of additional associated poor outcomes. Lessons learned Drawing insights from patient-level data at a population level is now possible, although doubt remain over quality at a more granular level. Defining parameters of our analysis was difficult and subjective, e.g. what is a poor outcome, given the constraints of the data." Ewan Evans, Graduate Data Scientist (Department for Health and Social Care) James Edholm, Senior Data Scientist (Department for Health and Social Care)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Developing the triple threat analyst
details: Introduction: What problem were you addressing? In this talk we want to showcase the modern “Triple Threat Analyst”. An analyst who combines traditional analytical skills, descriptive, to predictive to explicative analytics, with the ability to embrace modern developmental analytical techniques (i.e. Data science) and above all developing analysts to be involved in the process of prioritization and refinement of public health issues, all the way through to interpretation and presentation of information, and training decision makers to both fully understand and feel confident in the utilisation of data and intelligence in their work, both locally and nationally. Describe the aim, methods or approaches, and results In the talk we will showcase our LKIS approach and the apprentice programme. We will show how our mission to evolve the triple threat analyst create analysts who are able to adapt to modern analysis methods, software etc whilst being able to communicate their findings to all levels, and support decision makers, and others in the system to become excited and led by data and intelligence. Impact: How did your work influence decisions, policy, or learning? Whilst we cannot showcase impact as the apprenticeships are still running, we can show how analytical development needs to step away from traditional routes and position the analyst, and data and intelligence, right at the heart of explaining healthcare and wellbeing issues within populations. We want to show how analysis without the associated steps in prioritisation and explanation can create content which doesn’t land as powerfully as it could. Lessons learned: What would you do differently? We want attendees to think differently about the way they recruit, train and develop analysts within health and wellbeing, we want them to see the triple threat analyst as the future direction of travel for our analytical workforce, an aspirational goal which can only strengthen the position and quality of the workforce; an analyst who can analyse, code, explain, interpret, train and above all guide decision makers to become excited and influenced by data and intelligence. Isabelle Weeks, Public Health Intelligence Analyst (L7 Apprentice)(LKIS East of England ) James Harrison, Principal Knowledge Translator Facilitator
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Care Data Spaces
details: Local Authorities are facing pressure to use data effectively, but it's often difficult to know where to start, how to balance different needs, and how to make meaningful improvements in Adult Social Care. Even though Local Authorities collect and share social care data, it's often hard to access and not in a user-friendly format. Also, the heavy demand to provide care support makes it difficult for authorities to use this data to improve care and wellbeing. As a result, there are three main challenges: 1. Limited data insights into Adult Social Care. 2. Limited knowledge of what works best. 3. Reduced ability to develop data skills and learn. This presentation outlines ‘Care Data Spaces’ a collaborative, Open Science, data-driven research project between the ESRC Centre for Care at the University of Birmingham and West Midlands ADASS. The coproduced project (with people who receive support, their carers, commissioners, and decision makers) will build capacity and a modern data infrastructure to improve decision-making, social care support and wellbeing for people in the Adult Social Care system, and data literacy nationwide. The presentation outlines the following project elements: 1. Coproduction with people who have experience in social care, along with commissioners, practitioners, and policymakers, to develop a platform that can inform daily practice. 2. Collection and analysis of public Adult Social Care and geographic data to understand and improve Adult Social Care in Local Authorities. 3. Creation of customised reports for Local Authorities and an interactive website to support learning and decision-making. 4. Support for practitioners to integrate the platform into local authorities in the West Midlands and nationally. 5. Create learning resources to help people use the system to understand data better. Matt Bennett, Professor of Social Policy (University of Birmingham)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Developing a sustainability dashboard to drive data-driven action towards net zero
details: Introduction: The NHS is legally committed to achieve ambitious net-zero targets while balancing operational demands. At Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust (MFT), sustainability and carbon emissions data was fragmented, inconsistently processed, and not accessible to key decision-makers. This limited transparency, slowed progress, and hindered opportunities for site-level accountability. Aim: The project aimed to develop a centralised Sustainability Dashboard to improve data governance, enhance accessibility, and support evidence-based decision-making in pursuit of the Trust’s Green Plan commitments. Methods/Approach: The dashboard was designed iteratively in PowerBI, consolidating existing data streams (e.g., energy, waste, procurement, and medical gases) into interactive dashboards tailored for two user tiers: operational staff, and senior leadership. Collaborative workshops with Digital Estates, Pharmacy, and Transport teams shaped data governance, carbon factor consistency, and publishing processes. Training pathways (Microsoft PowerBI certification and NHS “Making Data Count”) were embedded to upskill the Sustainability Team and ensure project resilience. Results: While the iterative development is still ongoing, the dashboard has produced site-level sustainability insights for the first time, reducing manual data handling, increasing consistency, and enabling targeted analysis of carbon and cost “hotspots.” It streamlined reporting to statutory frameworks (e.g., ERIC), saving staff time and reducing duplication. Impact:The dashboard is influencing local decision-making by identifying opportunities for waste reduction and highlighting variation between sites. It has strengthened governance and accountability while creating co-benefits for pharmacy and estates teams through clearer, more actionable data. The impact will broaden as further elements of the carbon footprint are added. Lessons Learned: Early engagement across teams was critical for trust and alignment. Balancing ambition with capacity meant prioritising scalable, iterative development. In future, greater automation and student involvement could accelerate delivery while supporting workforce development. Megan Richold, Senior Sustainability Officer (Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust) Lida Fallah, Data Engineer (Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Using linked NHS datasets to rapidly generate insights into suicide deaths and prevention opportunities
details: Introduction: Suicide is a national public health priority, and prevention depends on understanding events leading to each death. Traditionally, insights come from manual case reviews, which are slow, resource-intensive, and hard to repeat. A faster, scalable, and cost-effective approach is needed to generate timely intelligence for prevention. Aim: Harness routinely collected NHS commissioning datasets to rapidly build a holistic picture of events leading to suicide and related demographic profiles, supporting targeted and data-driven prevention strategies. Methods: Using pseudonymised commissioning data, we built a longitudinal linked dataset on individuals in Birmingham and Solihull who died by suicide, capturing information from various health system contacts. We produced both aggregate statistics on system-wide patterns and individual-level timelines showing service interactions before death. The process, documented on GitHub, is simple to rerun regularly, providing up-to-date and repeatable intelligence. Results: Our analysis produced bespoke demographic insights into suicide deaths, offering a level of local intelligence not previously available. We found that 78% of individuals who died had some form of NHS contact in the year before death. There was wide variation in the type, frequency, and timing of interactions, highlighting potential missed opportunities for earlier intervention and support. A visual “case history on a page” was developed to summarise each person’s pathway, alongside population-level summaries showing patterns across services and demographics. Impact: This approach shows that actionable insights can be generated quickly and at low cost, providing a practical alternative to manual case reviews for the pan health and local authority Learning from Deaths group. It enables targeted, equity-focused suicide prevention planning and lays the groundwork for future cross-sector data integration. Lessons: NHS data alone can reveal important patterns, but a full understanding of suicide will require linking with wider social and economic datasets, and primary care data, to create a truly holistic view. Daniel Slater, Analyst and Data Visualisation Officer (Birmingham City Council) Harjrah Khan, Senior Public Health Officer (Birmingham City Council) David Ellis, Senior Data Scientist (Birmingham City Council)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Social return on investment - highlighting the value of PH interventions
details: The Problem Making Manchester Fairer (MMF) is a Manchester City Council initiative aimed at reducing health inequalities, which were starkly exposed during the COVID-19 pandemic. With increasing pressure on public finances, it’s essential to demonstrate that health interventions deliver meaningful value. Traditional cost-benefit analysis (CBA) focuses on financial returns but often misses wider social and personal impacts. MMF adopted a broader approach by incorporating social value—the real-life benefits people experience, such as improved mental wellbeing, stronger community connections, and better access to green spaces. Aim, Methods, and Results We used the Social Return on Investment (SROI) model to evaluate three MMF Kick-starter pilot projects targeting entrenched inequalities. SROI measures the value of outcomes that matter to stakeholders, not just financial metrics. It involves mapping inputs, outputs, and outcomes through an Impact Map (or theory of change), and calculating a social impact ratio. The approach is guided by seven principles, including stakeholder engagement, transparency, and materiality, ensuring the evaluation reflects lived experiences and priorities. Influence on Decisions and Policy The Year 1 SROI evaluation provided evidence to support a forecast for Years 2–4, strengthening the business case and guiding future investment decisions. It helped ensure that funding was aligned with interventions that deliver real, measurable impact. Lessons Learned Stakeholder engagement revealed unexpected insights and helped challenge inflated claims of impact. SROI encourages a realistic view of change and highlights what matters most to communities. We also learned that not every change needs to be tracked—if it can’t be measured reliably, it’s better to acknowledge that and focus on what can be evidenced. Martin Jennings, Performance C Insight programme Lead (Manchester City Council)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: From data to dialogue: A mixed-methods analysis to target NHS health check investment and reduce health inequalities in Birmingham.
details: Introduction: What problem were you addressing? The NHS Health Check is a key national preventative tool, yet significant uptake disparities persist among racially marginalised communities in Birmingham. Commissioners lacked granular, community-specific evidence to understand why uptake was low, hindering their ability to design effective interventions and target investment for maximum impact. Aim: To move beyond high-level statistics by using a participatory, mixed-methods approach to identify the specific barriers and facilitators to NHS Health Check uptake across ten of Birmingham's diverse ethnic communities, thereby generating actionable insights to inform local commissioning and service redesign. Methods or approaches used: The project was grounded in Participatory Action Research (PAR), collaborating with community-based providers to conduct focus groups with 193 participants. A double-layered sampling design captured insights across ethnicity, gender, and age. Quantitative demographic data was analysed for trends, while qualitative data was systematically analysed using Framework Analysis. Results: Quantitative analysis confirmed a statistically significant gap between eligible participants and the low number who had received a NHS Health Check. Thematic analysis revealed a profound lack of awareness as the primary barrier. Where awareness existed, misconceptions were common. Systematic barriers included ineffective communication (unclear letters), logistical challenges (inconvenient appointments), and a lack of culturally sensitive advice. Deep-seated mistrust was also a significant deterrent. Impact: How did your work influence decisions, policy, or learning? This analysis provides Birmingham City Council with a robust evidence base to shift from universal, 'one-size-fits-all' commissioning to targeted, data-driven investment. The findings directly inform the redesign of communication strategies and community-based delivery models to be more culturally competent and accessible, ensuring better value and impact from public health spending. Lessons learned: What would you do differently? The PAR model was highly effective for building trust and generating rich data. However, the process of co-designing research materials with ten community providers was time-intensive. In future projects, we would allocate a greater lead-in time for this co-design phase to further enhance collaboration from the very beginning. If this work has been presented elsewhere, please say so. This work has not been presented elsewhere. Dr Muhammad Hossain, Lecturer in Public Health (Birmingham City University)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Estimating MMR vaccine uptake in Birmingham and Solihull: Challenges and solutions
details: Introduction and aim: MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine uptake has been declining in Birmingham and Solihull in recent years, to the extent that 25% of five-year-olds in Birmingham had not received two doses of MMR in 2023/24. A measles outbreak in spring 2025 prompted renewed interest in defining vulnerable populations, to better target outreach including communications and immunisation clinics. Methods: Data was available on MMR uptake by LSOA, ethnicity, age, school and GP practice from various sources. First, the proportion and number of unvaccinated children (i.e. those had not received a first dose of MMR) were calculated at LSOA level and mapped as choropleth maps. This was repeated for five different ethnic groups at MSOA level. The proportion and number of unvaccinated pupils at each school was mapped as an interactive bubble map. Using data on uptake at various ages by GP practice, funnel plots were produced to identify GP practices with significantly higher or lower proportion of patients unvaccinated than average. Finally, GP-level data were aggregated to ward level using a weighted matrix and mapped as choropleth maps. Results: Variation in uptake across Birmingham and Solihull was considerable, with Birmingham (particularly central Birmingham) generally having a higher proportion of children unvaccinated. Several GPs were identified as having significantly high proportions of children unvaccinated. Impact: The maps produced will be used to inform where communications and interventions around MMR uptake should be targeted. The GP practices identified are being supported by Birmingham and Solihull ICB to improve vaccine uptake. Lessons learned: Despite having multiple data sources, coming to robust conclusions was challenging due to issues with data quality, timeliness and access. Better systems are needed to ensure access to data is maintained outside of outbreak scenarios. Evelyn Greeves, Analysis and Data Visualisation Officer (Birmingham City Council) Dr Carol Chatt, Consultant Epidemiologist and Head of Team Midlands (UK Health Security Agency) Leon Mallett, Head of Immunisations and Vaccinations (NHS Birmingham and Solihull)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Enhancing advanced analytics and leadership skills
details: Introduction: Our team’s learning and development programme has successfully upskilled the advanced analytical and leadership skills of all analysts, to meet the southeast region’s demand for prescriptive and predictive analytics and excellent stakeholder management and consultancy skills. Both are essential in improving patient outcomes, particularly through periods of significant change. Aim: To rapidly and equitably equip analysts with advanced analytical and leadership skills. Methods: We set a strategic vision and identified requisite key skills, including analytical tools (R/Python, Databricks, GitHub), techniques (forecasting, clustering) and leadership (communication, impact). The L&D team met regularly to support collaboration and accountability. The programme enabled everyone in the wider team to develop, within protected L&D time, via structured learning (10%), peer-mentoring (20%) and applying new skills on the job (70%). Each analyst facilitated one learning session each year. We tracked progress annually via National Competency Framework skills assessments, complemented by a detailed audit cycle. Gap analyses of calibrated results, against the original team-specific skill targets, informed the training programming. Results: All analysts lead senior stakeholder meetings, facilitate problem-solving, and deliver RAP-derived, statistically robust intelligence to inform decisions. We have upskilled the whole Analytics team to use GitHub, Databricks/UDAL, and forecast. Impact: Our analysts have the confidence to tackle steep learning curves together to acquire new skills. The scope of our analytical offerings is broader. Descriptive analytics are automated and RAP-based, and deeper-dive advanced forecasting and analytics are supporting patient care via the region’s systems and providers. Our approach fosters an open, psychologically safe culture and excellent analyst retention. Learning: An overt focus on L&D supports analysts to expand their skillsets. A combination of direct instruction, on-the-job learning and shared leadership opportunities are most effective in embedding new ways of working. Keiko Toma, Head of Analysis (NHS England) Charlotte Atherden, Regional Analyst (NHS England)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Breaking free from templates: Why analysts should trust themselves with custom CSS in Shiny Apps.
details: RShiny is increasingly being used by data analysts to share results and visualisations with peers, stakeholders, and the public. While RShiny is a powerful tool, default dashboard designs with many selectors and charts have the potential to overwhelm the user, often work poorly on mobile devices, and may be off-putting for policymakers, lay people, or healthcare professionals in a hurry. By breaking away from shinydashboard or bslib styling, and learning some fundamental web development tools, app designs have the potential to be much more flexible. Taking advantage of CSS allows analysts to align app design with their organisation's style guide, easing the transition from other web content, and building trust. With the rise of AI, learning new coding techniques is easier than ever. In this talk, we will showcase CRUK's Cancer Stats Data Hub, an app developed to share UK-level cancer incidence, mortality and survival statistics with healthcare professionals, but also used by analysts, policymakers, and the public. We will discuss our website-like design, developed in consultation with UX designers and informed by user testing. With specific examples, we will demonstrate how understanding CSS concepts like grid, flex, and media queries can transform the layout of Shiny apps and greatly improve functionality across a wide range of screen sizes, including mobile. We will discuss how the website-like Cancer Stats Data Hub allows for more timely updates for the analyst whilst, for the user, easing the transition from static web pages - reducing cognitive load and maintaining trust in the accuracy of content. Sam Finnegan, Senior Data and Research Analyst (Cancer Research UK) Matt Grant, Senior Data and Research Analyst (Cancer Research UK)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: WIDAC 2025: empowering women, strengthening the analytics profession
details: Introduction The future of health and care systems depends on analysts who are confident, visible, and equipped to shape decisions. Yet women remain under-represented in senior data and analytics roles, limiting equity and the diversity of perspectives that inform system decisions. The Women in Data & Analytics Conference (WIDAC) was created to change that: a regional initiative designed to empower professionals, strengthen networks, and build a replicable model for advancing the profession. Methods and Results WIDAC combined leadership keynotes, career development panels, wellness moments, and opportunities for connection. The 2025 launch drew 152 registrations from 45 organisations, with over 50 sign-ups in the first four days, demonstrating strong unmet demand. Of 33 survey respondents, 91% attended and nearly three-quarters reported feeling seen, heard, or represented. Feedback described the event as “warm and inclusive” and highlighted lessons in leadership, growth, and wellbeing. Senior NHS sponsorship and cross-sector collaboration added credibility and ensured relevance. Impact For professionals, WIDAC provided confidence, networks, and representation. For the profession, it showed how regional action can strengthen the analytical workforce, making it more diverse, resilient, and sustainable. For health and care systems, it demonstrated that empowering women analysts translates into richer insights and more equitable decision-making. To sustain impact, future iterations will add a technical webinar strand while keeping the main event people-first. Alongside WIDAC, the region also launched the Data & Analytics Managers’ Connect network, providing a complementary space for shared learning and leadership development. Lessons Learned Sponsorship and financial sustainability remain challenges; building a stronger funding model is a next step. Advertising could be clearer to extend reach. Most importantly, WIDAC confirmed that when analysts feel represented and supported, the whole system benefits — showing that investing in professional development is as vital as investing in data or technology. Louise Killen, Analytics Manager (Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust)"
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Whose application is it anyway? Building products for everyone in the UK Health and Care System
details: In the last ten years there has been an explosion in the number of ways to easily bring data science products to a wider audience. Typically a data scientist will build an application for a specific customer by prototyping and refining what they produce using customer feedback. But what happens when you're building something that you think has wide application but you don't have a relationship with every type of user yet and won't until the work is in a more complete state? What happens when you have a model or some code with multiple analytical groups working with it, borrowing and improving the modelling code and making their own applications on top of the existing code? This talk describes the first stages of bringing the disciplines of product and delivery to the work of a data science team and other allied analytical teams. The discipline of product has helped us to see our work through the eyes of users and to refine and extend our models and their interfaces to serve the needs of a diverse set of users. The discipline of delivery has helped us to respond flexibly and with agility, understanding and incorporating the work of other analysts and data scientists, maximising collaborative work and minimising duplication. You will leave the talk with a practical understanding of how to apply these lessons in your own work, whether you're leading a team of fifty or working on solo projects. Chris Beeley, Head of Data Science (Strategy Unit)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Calculating the cost of end-of-life care in the UK
details: Introduction More than 600,000 people die each year in the UK, of whom 90% could benefit from end-of-life (EOL) and palliative care. EOL care has had a limited profile compared with other pressures on the health system and public finances, which has profound implications for resource allocation decisions, particularly in the context of wider policy debate for this group of people. Aim Marie Curie commissioned Nuffield Trust and the Health Economics Unit to estimate the range of public expenditure that supports the care of people in their last year of life for the UK and each of the four nations. Methods We estimated expenditure using published data on service use and costs, and unpublished data provided from stakeholders. The three main areas of expenditure were healthcare, social care and social security. We identified information from a literature review and extensive stakeholder engagement, and assessed the impact of uncertainty in the results. Results In 2022 there was at least £22 billion public expenditure for people in the last year of life in the UK. Healthcare accounted for 53%, social care 22% and social security 25%. WE found that five times as much is spent on supporting people in the final year of life as hospital inpatients as support with primary care, community health and hospice care. The largest drivers of social care and social security expenditure are residential and nursing care, and pensions. Impact The analysis highlights the extent to which hospital expenditure exceeds the other areas, despite a long-standing policy goal of improving provision of EOL care in community settings. The findings were presented at a Parliamentary meeting and used as the basis of Marie Curie’s campaign to improve EOL care in the UK. Gayathri Kumar, Lead Health Economist (Health Economics Unit)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Assessing health inequalities for wait times to discharge in AsE at two hospital trusts in the West Midlands
details: Introduction Addressing health inequalities is important for improving health outcomes and equity within society. Following a paper from the Nuffield Trust examining wait times in A&E across equity themes, the Population Health Unit in Wolverhampton was asked to explore this for Walsall and Wolverhampton hospitals. Aim Analyse A&E wait times from arrival to departure across key equity themes including ethnicity, age, gender and deprivation. Expand on the univariate analysis from the Nuffield paper and advance analytical practice locally by using AI to explore multivariate techniques. Identify if there are any key variables that impact on wait time. Methods A&E data was extracted from an SQL database and wrangled. Alongside the key equity variables, other variables including arrival method, day and time, season, acuity and discharge method were used. Data was analysed in excel, then R and Python for more advanced statistical techniques. Machine learning techniques used were regression, random forest and gradient boost. Results and impact Univariate analysis showed some equity themes had longer waits, however, multivariate analysis demonstrated that once adjusting for confounders, access in terms of wait times was broadly equitable. Key variables that impacted on wait time to discharge were, whether admitted, acuity, age and arrival hour. Results were presented at the Joint Health Inequalities Board, the learning from this project was valuable to reassure about access equity at A&E regarding wait times. Further work was proposed to look at other potential equity issues in A&E, such as those leaving prior to assessment. Findings were also included in the Trusts health inequalities annual report. As multiple software was used this resulted in storage and processing limitations. To improve data wrangling, efficiency and replication, next time, it would be desirable to use R and Python throughout, linking directly to SQL, then performing the univariate and multivariate analysis. Karla Bailey, Senior Population Health Intelligence Specialist (The Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust) Jason Gwinnett, Principal Population Health Intelligence Specialist (The Royal Wolverhampton NHS FT)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Multidisciplinary analytical pipelines: Productionising a business critical simulation model
details: Our data science team has been engaged for some time productionising a simulation model whose function is to predict demand for acute hospital care. Providing the functionality required to make the model easy to use, reliable, and quick in use has posed a considerable challenge, as has building, maintaining, and keeping updated this model while it is being used by a range of users with different needs. This talk will explore firstly how the team tackled this with data science methods as well as by using the full range of skills within a multidisciplinary analytic team. Running the model required a range of data science technologies, including cloud compute and storage, Docker, R and Python code, applications, R/ Shiny, and databricks. The project is by the NHS, for the NHS- all of the code has been released under an open source licence and the model was recently awarded the Florence Nightingale award. It takes a village to ship a model, and the talk will also describe the work of the multidisciplinary team who worked on the model- working on its design, analytical questions which came from the results and parameters, user researchers, and a team to train and guide users of the model to assist them in high quality modelling to support the model's use in business cases. We believe in designing, productionising, and open sourcing high quality models and other tools to support analysis and decision making by the NHS, for the NHS. This talk will describe our evolving approach to meet the needs of stakeholders across the health and care system in this and other contexts. Chris Beeley, Head of Data Science (Strategy Unit)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Not normal:Extending synthetic difference-in- differences to non-gaussian outcomes
details: This presentation focusses on the methods and results of an impact evaluation of a large national programme which invested £30 million pounds over five years across more than 35 sites to improve clinical outcomes for a specific at-risk and socially marginalized group*. From the perspective of the evaluation, the key challenges were that the programme was specifically targeted at areas with the highest level of need, meaning that most areas unaffected by the programme had very few of the target group relative to areas affected by the programme, hindering direct comparison. Furthermore, while the targeted group is associated with highly elevated level of need in relative terms, they make up a relatively small number in absolute terms. This evaluation used a variation of synthetic difference-in-differences to evaluate the programme’s impact on clinical outcomes. As the total number of affected people within any given area at a given time was small, and modelling errors were likely to be highly non-normal for structural reasons, standard SDID methods (such as the r package synthdid) are likely to give biased estimates. The method used in this analysis builds on standard methods by extending the SDID methodology to be used with count data and rate data (based on the poisson and binomial distributions respectively). This presentation will provide a brief motivation to the method, with a focus on a worked example of its use, as applied to A&E admissions by the target group (which were found to have been statistically significantly reduced by the programme). All code associated with the method will be released on GitHub by the time of the presentation, allowing others to apply the method in similar scenarios. *permission has been requested to name the programme, although at the time of submission has not yet been granted Andre Bilbrough, Healthcare Analyst (Strategy Unit)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Transforming Health Needs Assessments: Reproducible insights for smarter NHS planning
details: Introduction: Health Needs Assessments (HNAs) are central to understanding population health and guiding Integrated Care Board (ICB) planning, but they are often delivered as static reports. These can be difficult to update, lack transparency, and limit opportunities for interactive exploration. Our aim was to develop a reproducible, scalable, and interactive approach to HNAs using open-source tools. Methods/Approach: We used R for data integration, analysis, and visualisation, and Quarto for publishing an interactive report. This unified workflow captures the entire process—from data preparation through to reporting—ensuring that every step is reproducible, auditable, and easily updated. The modular design supports scalability across different ICBs and health domains, while interactive dashboards and drill-down tools enable users to explore inequalities, demographic trends, and service utilisation in depth. Results/Impact: The project demonstrates how an HNA can be transformed from a static document into a living, dynamic resource for population health management and planning. This approach improves consistency, reduces duplication, and enhances usability for analysts, planners, and clinicians. It has the potential to shape how population health intelligence is produced and used, supporting more agile and equitable decision-making across the NHS. Lessons learned: Early engagement with stakeholders was critical in shaping the design and functionality of the interactive HNA. Future iterations will focus on streamlining deployment across multiple ICB geographies and embedding training to build confidence in using reproducible workflows. Rachel Christie, Senior Population Analyst (North West London ICB)
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: National Competency Framework for Data Professionals: Version 3
details: Launched in October 2023, this National Competency Framework for data professionals framework is now in its second version and work is already under way for version three. New roles, new specialisms and the first ever definition of a domain will all form part of the next iteration. Our goal was to create a dynamic tool that evolves with the changes in the data and analytics workforce, ensuring it remains relevant and effective. We update the framework annually to reflect new roles and skill sets. This ensures the Framework stays relevant to your community. Keeping at its core the principle of an open, transparent and collaborative development approach, we continually listen and engage with the wider community to ensure you can access the latest competencies for your development. The framework has already been adopted by about 25% of organisations in health and care across the country, making it a robust and replicable tool for others to use. The framework is seen as a significant support in the move of the analytics workforce to the high intensity outputs required to support the Fit for the Future 10 year plan. By providing a structured path for career progression, it is helping shape strategies to develop a more skilled and effective data and analytics workforce. The insights gained from the framework are instrumental in the move toward a formally recognised professional data and analytics workforce We know the importance of continuous engagement with the data and analytics community. Future updates will be drawn from your feedback and help shape the career development of analysts now and in the future using a consistent nationally recognised approach. We will share what is coming in Version 3, what successes have been seen to date and how anyone in the analytical community can adopt the Framework and begin their journey to professional development. Andrew Lavelle, Senior Manager Analytical Professionalisation (NHS England) Sarah Blundell, Data and Analytical Development Lead (NHS England)"
collection: HACA - Health and Care Analytics Conference

title: Making national cancer audit reporting shiny: A journey from Excel to web-based apps using r and reproducible analytical pipelines
details: National cancer audits play a key role in monitoring care quality and driving NHS service improvement. The National Cancer Audit Collaborating Centre (NATCAN) reports cancer audit results for 120 providers in England and six in Wales. Historically, provider-level results were distributed as manually prepared Microsoft Excel files, with limited visualisation of trends over time or interactivity. Increasing our reporting frequency from annual to quarterly required greater efficiency in our way of working. To address these challenges, NATCAN selected the National Lung Cancer Audit (NLCA) to pilot quarterly publication of provider-level results via a web-based, Shiny application. Methods: The Shiny application was built using open source tools (R) and Reproducible Analytical Pipeline principles, with learnings applied from NHS-R workshops. External stakeholder consultation informed design of the user interface and downloadable parameterised reports. Agile development cycles enable iterative development, with new features informed by user feedback to ensure it meets their needs. Reproducible results are generated through scripts, ensuring an automated data pipeline that produces consistent outputs when rerun on new data. Open access to dashboards (no login), with all tables and figures available for download, ensures provider-level results can be used and built-on by others. Scalability is ensured through deployment to a managed cloud environment, which maintains app performance as user numbers increase. Webinars, co-hosted with professional societies, demonstrated dashboard functionality to support dissemination and familiarisation among providers. Results, impact and lessons learned: Engagement has doubled since moving NLCA provider-level results from Excel to Shiny. This successful pilot project led to all ten national cancer audits within NATCAN moving to Shiny. Sharing modular code across audits enabled 90% to launch within three months, delivered efficiencies in quarterly reporting and freed analyst time for other priorities. Focus group feedback highlighted how dashboards have better supported data-driven decision-making for providers. Ella Barber, Data Scientist (National Cancer Audit Collaborating Centre)

title: Is AI ready to transform evidence reviews in the NHS?
details: Background: The Health Economics Unit was commissioned by ICB partners to identify valuable evidence from more than 38,000 publications. Working collaboratively with stakeholders, we agreed to trial an AI-assisted methodology to test whether it could deliver a faster and reproducible review. Aim: Our aim was to identify interventions with proven cost-saving potential in NHS and care settings, with a particular focus on the NHS ‘Three Shifts’ (moving care from hospitals to communities, leveraging digital innovation, and emphasising prevention). We sought to test whether an AI-assisted review method could achieve this at scale. Methodology: We built a Python-based framework integrating OpenAI’s GPT-4o to screen a database of references from peer-reviewed and grey literature. Staged prompts applied NHS-focused criteria to identify studies reporting cost outcomes, comparators, and evidence of cash savings, improving accuracy and efficiency compared with traditional reviews. In collaboration with an expert researcher, a manually screened validation dataset was developed to fine-tune prompts, identify discrepancies, and measure accuracy at each stage of screening. Results: The screening pipeline reduced 5,175 references to 186 studies. QA showed that this was as accurate as human screening, demonstrating proof of concept for using AI to improve the speed, quality and efficiency of literature reviews. Outputs were presented in a short report and interactive evidence map, enabling users to explore by type, setting, and financial impact. Identified examples included clinical service changes reducing admissions and treatment costs, digital platforms delivering measurable prescribing and mental health savings, and prevention programmes that lowered overall expenditure. Conclusion/Impact: AI-assisted screening can process evidence at scale, but there remains a need for targeted human validation to capture nuance and ensure confidence in outputs. Together, this approach supports faster decision-making and offers a scalable model for future evidence reviews. Oliver Carey, Data Scientist/Econometrician (Health Economics Unit)

title: NIHR Academy - Career Development Opportunities for Data Science in Health and Care
details: This Insight talk introduces the career development programmes available through the NIHR Academy - with a particular focus towards funding support for those using Data Science tools and methods for health and care research. Chris and Kieran cover the range of opportunities across all career stages, clinical and non-clinical and the talk is suitable for quantitative researchers from non-NIHR backgrounds who are considering research in these areas. Part of the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), the NIHR Academy attracts, trains and supports health and care researchers at all stages of their careers, from predoctoral through to chair. A wide range of funding opportunities are available comprising personal fellowship awards, shorter training and development support as well as opportunities funded at the institutional level, including through NIHR infrastructure centres, NIHR Schools and wider NIHR capacity building structures.
collection: SWAIH - South West Analytics and Infrastructure in Healthcare

title: IPACS - Improving Patient Flow between Acute, Community and Social Care
details: This talk introduces the IPACS project - exploring how to optimize capacity for complex patient discharge pathways and understand how to alleviate the shortage of acute beds that results from any delays in discharge to social care . Transferring patients from hospitals to their homes or temporary care facilities is a complicated process that requires both efficient planning and effective support. However, delays and capacity issues often disrupt this process, especially when there isn’t enough care available in the right place at the right time. Social care shortages, as the final step in the care chain, are a major contributor to these delays. In 2019 alone, delays caused by unavailable social care led to the loss of about 500,000 acute hospital bed days in England. Researchers from the Universities of Bath and Exeter collaborated with healthcare managers in local NHS Trusts to create an open-source simulation tool coded in R. Links to the GitHub repository are included in the talk. This adaptable and free tool models discharge pathways, known as ‘Discharge to Assess’ (D2A), and helps predict demand, capacity, and patient stay durations. By simulating scenarios, it can directly support decision-making for improving D2A services and managing seasonal pressures like winter demand.
collection: SWAIH - South West Analytics and Infrastructure in Healthcare
